#4459. NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover breaks historic record after traveling 28 miles

NASA's Perseverance rover has reached an impressive new milestone, traveling farther across another world than any vehicle before it. On Sol 2006 (Oct. 11, 2026), the rover's total driving distance reached 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles), establishing a new record for travel on another celestial body. The achievement was even recognized by Guinness World Records, which presented a commemorative plaque to Perseverance's engineering twin on Earth.

The rover had actually come close to breaking the record about two months earlier. On Sol 1947, Perseverance was just 200 meters short of the milestone, a distance it could have covered in a single trip using its Autonomous Navigation (AutoNav) system.

But reaching the record was not the team's immediate priority. Perseverance was exploring an area filled with scientifically valuable ancient rock formations, so it spent weeks making short trips between locations to examine exposed rock surfaces. These investigations included grinding away thin layers of rock and conducting detailed measurements up close. Once the scientific work was complete, the rover resumed its journey and soon surpassed the previous distance record.

"Two months ago, (Perseverance) sat about 200 meters away from the milestone, a distance easily achievable with a single drive... However, the rover found itself in a very scientifically interesting area and spent time (investigating) ancient rock outcrops. When Perseverance was finally ready to move on to a new site, it sailed past the record."

How NASA Improved Perseverance's Driving Capabilities

Covering more than 28 miles on Mars has required Perseverance to overcome difficult terrain while testing new approaches to robotic driving. Its journeys through tightly packed boulder fields and across steep hillsides have given NASA engineers valuable experience, helping them improve the rover's ability to navigate hazardous landscapes.

To expand what Perseverance can safely handle, engineers conducted thousands of computer simulations and adjusted several operating limits. The rover can now tolerate tilts of up to 24 degrees, while the minimum clearance beneath its protective belly pan has been reduced to 20 centimeters (about 7.9 inches).

The team also introduced several important improvements to the driving system. Updated braking software helps the rover avoid collisions with rocks, and the electrical current limits for its steering motors have been nearly doubled. Engineers also added "dynamic slip tables" to its flight software, allowing the rover to better anticipate how much its wheels might slip on different surfaces.

Another technique involves driving across slopes in ways that help keep the wheels securely positioned on exposed bedrock. Together, these changes allow Perseverance to handle challenging terrain more effectively as it continues exploring Mars.

A Mars Rover That Can Navigate Without GPS

Among the rover's most significant technological advances is a system called onboard Global Localization (GBLC). This technology gives Perseverance a way to determine its position on Mars without relying on directions from Earth.

The system uses a powerful commercial processor originally installed in the Ingenuity Helicopter Base Station. By comparing images captured from the Martian surface with pictures taken from orbit, it can calculate the rover's location in global coordinates after completing a drive (as though we had GPS on a world without it).

Knowing its position independently is a major advantage. It allows Perseverance to cover greater distances without needing people on Earth to repeatedly determine its location, potentially making future exploration faster and more efficient.

However, this approach introduced an engineering challenge. Unlike the rover's main flight computer, the additional processor was not specifically designed to withstand the intense radiation conditions on Mars. The planet has a thin atmosphere and no global magnetic field, leaving electronics exposed to radiation that can interfere with their operation.

In particular, radiation can cause "transient bit flips" that unexpectedly change information stored in computer memory, potentially disrupting software. To address this problem, engineers developed software protections that help the processor operate reliably despite the harsh environment.

The Next Frontier in Autonomous Mars Exploration

NASA is also investigating how generative AI could make the rover even more independent. As missions involve longer journeys and increasingly complex operations, the team wants to reduce the time and resources needed to plan safe routes.

The technology could help generate driving plans for the many individual segments of a longer journey, providing guidance that Perseverance's AutoNav system can use to navigate the terrain.

After traveling 45 kilometers (more than 28 miles), Perseverance has already provided engineers with extensive experience in navigating the Martian landscape. Those lessons are now shaping new technologies that could transform how robotic explorers operate on distant worlds.

And the journey is far from over. As Perseverance continues climbing higher along the rim of its Martian crater, NASA is preparing for the next major advances in autonomous exploration.

Materials provided by NASA. Original written by Vandi Verma, Chief Engineer for Robotic Operations at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4458. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Review: Everything Switch Sports Should Have Been

Wuhu Island is back, and so is the magic. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort finally recaptures the charm that made me fall for this series years ago.

Say Nintendo Switch Sports Resort three times in a row. Go on, I’ll wait. It’s a tongue twister of a title, and I tripped over it every single time, which is at complete odds with the smoothness the game delivered.

The Nintendo DS didn’t just have great games, it had ideas that stuck around way longer than anyone expected.

I have played every entry in this series. When the Wii turned waving a remote around the living room into a whole new way of playing, I was right there, and I’ve had a soft spot for motion controls ever since. I do enjoy a good sports game, but if I’m honest, it’s mostly Nintendo’s that get me off the sofa. That’s also why I always worry a little whenever a new one is announced, because Nintendo Switch Sports never quite managed to feel like the series I fell in love with.

DualShockers was given a code for this review, and I’ve spent multiple hours on Wuhu Island so far, mostly in single player, on a docked Switch 2. I am nowhere near 100%, and I suspect that could take hundreds of hours depending on how good you are. But the hours I have put in have been more than enough to know this is the game I wanted Switch Sports to be.

The first thing I noticed was how little I was waiting. Load times are much shorter than in Nintendo Switch Sports, menus snap into place, and you can even rearrange the layout of the sports to suit you. Everything feels smoother, less clunky and quicker to get going. After the last entry, that alone felt like a small miracle.

Nintendo games always feel good, and I went in with high expectations of polish. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort met every single one of them. It ran perfectly on my docked Switch 2, and I didn’t run into a single bug or crash in my time playing this. Why can’t every game feel this polished?

My first birdie in Golf and my first strike in Bowling both made me grin like an idiot. It turns out the muscle memory I built up over years of these games is fully transferable, and it all just feels a bit more refined now. Bowling and Golf are still my favourites, Table Tennis gives you lovely control over every return, and Archery is so satisfying that I kept going back for “just one more” target. Tennis now comes with three courts to choose from, which is nice, if hardly a revolution.

Not everything landed quite as well. Boxing was the one I enjoyed least, because the Joy-Con 2 occasionally lost track of me once I mixed in ducks, hooks and jabs. Volleyball, unfortunately, still feels very sluggish, and that carries over into online play, too. It’s my single biggest deduction, and it’s a shame, because Volleyball also gave me one of my favourite moments.

Picture this: deuce after deuce, a match that seemingly will not end, my arms burning. By the time it was over, I was panting and had to sit down and rethink a few of my life choices. Nintendo, if you’re reading this, I desperately need a new Ring Fit Adventure, because that game actually kept me fit.

Then there’s Thumb Wrestling. It’s such an odd addition, and it makes me laugh every time, because it is so very Nintendo. It’s simple to pick up, there’s more strategy to it than you’d ever expect, and I can already see it causing chaos at parties. And yet.

I cannot believe they included Thumb Wrestling over my beloved Baseball. I’d have taken Disc Golf from the original Wii Sports Resort, too. Some of the racket and net sports also start to blur together after a while, so a little more variety would have gone a long way.

My favourite part of Resort is the trio of Leisure Sports, which have nothing to do with winning and everything to do with simply enjoying the island. Power Cruising puts you on a jet ski, with a Joy-Con held sideways like handlebars, twisting to accelerate and leaning to steer. Prop Plane turns your controller into a little aeroplane in your hand, and Skateboarding uses mouse mode, so you swipe across the table to push off and flick upwards for tricks. Luckily, the Nintendo Switch 2’s Welcome Tour trained me for exactly that moment. Generally, these sports are the most creative controls in the whole game, and they’re where I spent a lot of my down time.

Each of them comes with a Sightseeing Tour, where you have five minutes to explore and collect as much as you can. I’ll admit the timer sometimes had me wishing for more. There is a Free Roam mode without one, but none of the collectibles appear there, so it’s more of a scenic drive than a treasure hunt.

There’s no story in Resort, not really, but the sightseeing is the closest it gets. Finding photo spots and cruising past corners of Wuhu Island I’d never seen before taught me more about the place than any previous entry. It’s also the perfect palate cleanser after a sweaty round of Volleyball.

Hyrule has never looked better as they look in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, and critics seem to agree!

Very quickly I discovered probably the number one reason that will keep me playing for months: everything counts now. In Nintendo Switch Sports, you could only earn the points needed to unlock new outfits and accessories by playing online. In Switch Sports Resort, every game you finish earns you points, single player included, and you spend them in a shop that rotates its collections weekly and monthly. You don’t even need a Nintendo Switch Online Membership anymore!

What you can pull from the shop is random and different for every user. It covers clothes, accessories, name tag options and sporting gear. On top of that, each sport has its own achievements, which you can unlock solo or with friends. As a bit of an achievement collector, that’s dangerous news for my free time.

For anyone who wants more of a challenge, Island Crown sets you up against increasingly skilled CPU players in each sport, with an Island Champ waiting at the top. The first few opponents are almost charmingly bad, but the tougher ones are genuinely tough. Nintendo has also added a little more “canon” this time, with each sport’s champion getting a bit of backstory. I haven’t beaten a single Champ yet, but I’m working on it.

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort looks gorgeous. It’s bursting with colour and that typical Nintendo charm, and I never once got tired of looking at it. The soundtrack is upbeat and light-hearted, and returning players will recognise plenty of the sound cues. My favourite detail? In Golf, you can hear the waves crashing against the shore and birds chirping between your shots.

The island itself never feels empty. Miis stroll around in the background, and even the CPU opponents use the little stickers that are the game’s only way of communicating. You can play as the newer-style characters and the classic Miis, which made me happier than I’d like to admit. Every session left me feeling a little brighter, which is exactly what I want from this series.

Accessibility has taken a step forward, too. You can choose your dominant hand for every sport, turn on a colourblind mode, and switch off the emote pop-ups from other players and CPUs if you find them distracting. Golf has assistance options, and the tutorials are clear and helpful. You are still tied to the Joy-Cons and motion controls, though: there are no alternative control schemes, and nothing can be remapped.

This is a game for literally everyone. If you just want some fun, need something to play with your family or friends, or want an excuse to move a bit more, this game has you covered. You can play with one to four people locally, go online, take on CPU opponents, and even team up with a CPU partner in some sports. I can already see it becoming the focal point of many a games night.

What surprised me most is how good it is on your own. It’s the most fun I’ve had in a while, even playing completely alone. Games like this usually lose steam once the novelty wears off, but there’s so much variety here that I’m nowhere near running out of things to do.

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort looks gorgeous. It’s bursting with colour and that typical Nintendo charm, and I never once got tired of looking at it.

Online play does have a couple of bumps in typical Nintendo fashion. Bowling has some strange waits between turns, and switching sports kicks you back to the lobby. These are pretty small complaints, though, when everything around them is this good. If anything, Nintendo has undersold this one: for how much better it is than its predecessor, it deserved a much bigger marketing push.

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is a great revival for a series I’m always a little worried about. Nintendo is one of the only AAA players left that still brings real whimsy to the table, and Resort feels fresh, special, and complete from day one. If you want a sports game with actual substance, rather than a handful of minigames, this is the one. If you’d rather sink into a big story, look elsewhere – and if you hate fun? Honestly, I’m not sure how you ended up reading a review about Wii Sports' cheerful grandchild, but I admire the commitment. Somewhere on Wuhu Island, an Island Champ is waiting for me. I might not be ready yet. But I want to become the Island Legend, so I will keep training.

#4457. Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think

Carrying excess weight may affect more than physical health. New research from the University of Georgia suggests that having a higher body mass index may also speed up cognitive decline, potentially causing memory and thinking abilities to deteriorate more quickly with age.

Some cognitive changes are a natural part of getting older. Remembering information, thinking clearly, and processing new details can become more difficult over time. For healthy adults, however, these changes are usually relatively mild and develop gradually.

The new findings suggest that excess body weight may accelerate this process. Researchers found that people with higher body mass index (BMI) experienced faster declines in memory, overall cognitive performance, and executive functioning. These abilities are essential for everyday activities such as concentrating, planning, organizing tasks, and regulating emotions.

To investigate the connection, the research team analyzed data from a nationally representative study that tracked more than 8,200 adults over age 50 for 24 years.

Higher BMI Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline

The results revealed a consistent relationship between body weight and cognitive health. Each one-point increase in BMI was associated with a faster rate of cognitive decline, suggesting that even relatively small differences in body weight could matter over time.

The association was strongest at the eighth year of the study, and adults older than 65 showed the most pronounced effects.

Despite the concerning findings, researchers also identified a potentially encouraging opportunity to protect brain health. Managing body weight may help slow cognitive decline, with possible benefits becoming apparent within just two years.

"We found that if people managed their weight, they could significantly lower their rate of cognitive decline in just two years," said Suhang Song, the study's lead author and an assistant professor at the University of Georgia's College of Public Health. "That makes BMI one of the most easily modifiable risk factors when it comes to aging well."

How Excess Weight May Affect the Aging Brain

Obesity, generally defined as a BMI of 30 or higher, has been associated with poorer brain health. However, scientists are still working to understand exactly why carrying excess body weight may interfere with memory and other cognitive abilities.

Several biological processes could help explain the connection. Excess weight may promote inflammation, impair blood circulation, and contribute to insulin resistance. Together, these changes could increase the likelihood of cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, and other forms of dementia.

The findings are particularly relevant given how widespread obesity has become in the United States. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately two in five Americans meet the criteria for obesity when BMI is used as the sole measure.

Some scientists argue that BMI alone does not provide a complete picture of obesity. They support a broader definition that also considers waist measurements and medical conditions associated with excess weight. Using those additional criteria, the estimated proportion of Americans classified as having obesity rises to 75%.

Weight Management Could Help Protect Brain Health

The potential connection between obesity and cognitive decline is especially concerning as dementia becomes increasingly common. More than 7 million Americans currently live with dementia, and researchers expect that number to double by 2050.

Although the study does not establish that excess weight directly causes cognitive decline, its findings highlight body weight as a potentially important factor in maintaining cognitive health. Because weight can be managed, researchers believe it could offer an opportunity to reduce the risk of worsening memory and thinking abilities as people grow older.

"There are no cures for dementia," Song said, "which is why it is critical to identify and address any modifiable risk factors we can find to prevent it."

The research was published in the Journal of Neurology. Coauthors from the University of Georgia College of Public Health include Meng Hsuan Sung, Zhuo Chen, Janani Rajbhandari, Grace Bagwell Adams, Mahmud Khan, Ye Shen, and Xiao Song. Qianhui Xu and Xia Song also contributed to the study.

#4455. This Focus RS Makes Us Nostalgic for a Time When Ford Built Cars Besides the Mustang

This hot hatch has just 2200 miles and is being sold by the original owner on Bring a Trailer.

Ford killed off the Focus globally just last year, much to the chagrin of anyone who enjoyed a scrappy little hatchback or sedan with a blue oval up front. Sure, the Mustang is still around, but the Focus and the Fiesta provided an entirely different kind of Fast Ford, compact performance that you could use every day. And there was one Focus trim that was the best of them all.

Here’s a nearly new example of maximum Focus: a 2016 Focus RS with just 2200 miles on the odometer, for sale on Bring a Trailer (which, like Car and Driver, is part of Hearst Autos). It’s a single-owner, garage-kept car from Texas, and for those in colder climes, it happens to have been optioned with the RS2 package that includes heated seats and a heated steering wheel. Slap on a set of snow tires, and get ready to shred this upcoming winter.

See all results for used 2016 Ford Focus RS for sale near 66502

Pairing a 350-hp 2.3-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine with a six-speed manual gearbox and clever all-wheel drive, the Focus RS was basically Ford’s answer to the Subaru STI and the Mitsubishi Lancer EVO. WRC champion Colin McRae did spend quite a bit of time rallying in Fords, and that heritage was baked right into the RS, even if U.S. fans weren’t as broadly familiar with the world of rally.

For those who were, the RS was a revelation. The punchy four built boost quickly, and it somehow had far more turbo personality than when it appeared in the EcoBoost version of the Mustang. The all-wheel drive was even better, equipped with the ability to direct as much as 70 percent of the power to either outside rear wheel. With understeer thus banished, the RS could tear up a winding back road with a pace equal to far more expensive machines.

And yes, it came with Drift mode. Fully unlock this ability by switching off traction control, and the Focus RS can lay down Ken Block–style tire-smoking slides with ease. Not great for your tire budget, but huge fun nonetheless.

The only drawback was trying to get your hands on one when new, as dealers often tried to add considerable markup to the price tag. This example, painted a laid-back Stealth Gray, flies under the radar a bit and is just waiting for an owner who is going to pack on the miles.

In a low-key color, and with only hints of the performance peeking out from that hatchback shape in the form of a rear wing and blue Brembo brakes, this RS is a bit of an if-you-know-then-you-know car. It’s a real shame that Ford doesn’t sell anything like it anymore. On the other hand, that just makes this one that much more special.

#4454. Gentle Mates GC come from a map down to beat Shopify Rebellion Gold and reach Game Changers final

Gentle Mates GC, on their Championship debut, beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 2-1 in the upper bracket final in São Paulo. The French-based side go into Sunday's best-of-five grand final with a two-map ban advantage, while Shopify Rebellion Gold must come through the lower final.

Gentle Mates GC are into the grand final of the VCT Game Changers Championship 2026. They beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 2-1 in the upper bracket final in São Paulo on Friday 30 October. The French-based side dropped the opening map and then took the next two. Both teams had arrived at the match with every map at the event won.

Shopify Rebellion Gold won map one, which lasted 53 minutes. On the second map they fought back to 10-10, but Gentle Mates closed it out 13-11 after 55 minutes. The decider on Summit ran for 57 minutes and finished 13-10 to Gentle Mates.

Coming through the upper bracket gives Gentle Mates a two-map ban advantage in the grand final. Shopify Rebellion Gold, led at the event by interim in-game leader alexis, drop into the lower bracket final against KRÜ Blaze.

This is Gentle Mates’ first appearance at the Championship. Their line-up of Marti, Nami, Wens, tokameite and berryx reached the upper final with 2-0 wins over Team Liquid Brazil and MIBR GC. Their last three EMEA Stage 3 results before the event were wins over G2 Gozen and SK Nebula, both 2-1, and a 3-2 defeat to G2 Gozen.

The Elo power rankings already had Gentle Mates ahead. They sit fourth with a rating of 1844 and a 33-7 record from 40 rated matches. Shopify Rebellion Gold are sixth on 1809, with a 40-20 record from 60 rated matches.

Shopify Rebellion Gold had cleared SK Nebula and KRÜ Blaze without losing a map. Before travelling, they beat FlyQuest RED 3-1 and 2-1 and SwimTrek Blue 2-0 in North America Stage 2. At last year’s Championship in Seoul, Team Liquid Brazil beat them 3-2 in the title match.

The lower bracket final is a rematch. Shopify Rebellion Gold beat KRÜ Blaze in the upper semi-final. KRÜ then earned their place with lower bracket wins over Team Liquid Brazil and MIBR GC, both without dropping a map. MIBR GC finished fourth, which is worth $50,000. SK Nebula, one of three EMEA teams in São Paulo, placed joint fifth to sixth for $25,000. Their line-up included Scottish player fluxxy.

ON VA EN FINALE DES WORLDS ! pic.twitter.com/vAt2vVdyvY

Third place pays $70,000. The lower bracket final and the grand final are both best-of-five, after best-of-three series in the earlier rounds of the double-elimination bracket. Ten teams entered the event at Riot Games Arena, which Riot describes as the last Game Changers Championship to be held as a standalone event. In 2027 the Championship moves to Austin, Texas. For the first time it will run in the same city at the same time as VALORANT Champions, from 16 September to 10 October.

Shopify Rebellion Gold and KRÜ Blaze meet in the lower bracket final on Saturday 31 October at 15:00 BRT. The winner faces Gentle Mates GC in the grand final on Sunday 1 November at 15:00 BRT.

#4452. Chauffeur Life

My guests’ expertise in rear-seat amenities provides some insight into passenger-pleasing design.

The kids sure like to drink. Just not alcohol. Data shows that’s down by a considerable percentage among young people. Good for them. No, the youths in my social circle like to stay hydrated. They are never without a water bottle (bedazzled or stickered to set it apart from everyone else’s Owalas and Stanleys) or a sweet tea with a fat straw from a boba shop.

On a recent weekend visit from my college bestie and her teen and tween daughters, we must have hit every bubble-beverage and smoothie spot in town. All of that chauffeuring made me hyperaware of what makes for a well-appointed back seat. Number one, according to my expert passengers? Cupholders. Not just for drinks, but also for phones and sunglasses, because it’s easier to remember them when they’re sticking up rather than hiding inside a console or lying on a charging pad. Note to designers: Can you do phone-charging cupholders?

The Ford Ranger that I had for the weekend got high marks for its back-seat cupholders and the fold-down console with its padded armrest. “I hate when there’s nowhere to lean,” declared the 16-year-old, weary already. It’s exhausting being so cool.

See all results for used cars for sale near 90017

Complaints about the Ranger were the lack of dedicated climate vents for the back seat—their mother and I were freezing up front while they were still too warm in the back—and the hefty step-up into the cabin, which was challenging while carrying a large milk tea with mango jelly. “I can’t hold the door and jump down at the same time,” the younger one said, exhibiting a remarkable concern for parking-lot door dings rarely shown by people who don’t pay insurance premiums (and often not even by those who do).

A later ride in my ’80s Dodge Ramcharger had the same step-up and A/C problems, but the couchlike bench seat and full-length windows offset the lack of modern amenities. That vehicle is a favorite of my neighbor’s kids too, so if you’re investing in collector cars, grab a Ramcharger or a Plymouth Trail Duster before they go the way of vintage Broncos in price.

While trucks from that era might seem like a potential family travel solution, not everyone is willing to let their kids ride in a vehicle where the closest things to airbags are the Gabriel HiJackers someone installed in 1973 and the whoopee cushion that’s been under the seat since two owners ago. With that in mind, I made a list of some modern back-seat luxuries that have impressed me or my discerning young friends in recent new cars.

Dual Bluetooth connectivity: Unless you like being critiqued for your playlist, the ideal setup lets a back-seat passenger connect their phone for media while the driver links theirs for ­navigation­ and­ communication.­ I ­first ­noticed­ this ­feature ­on a Dodge Durango, but it’s increasingly common in newer infotainment systems.

See all results for used cars for sale near 90017

Third-row USB ports: It’s pretty much a given that second rows will have charging points, but with bigger families, that middle row is where the child safety seats latch in. While little ones might run low on apple juice, the older crew in the wayback will require a different kind of recharge. If you’re looking at base models, make sure to check the USB-port placement, as those are the trims most likely to cheap out on the third row.

Smart seats: I recently drove the new long-wheelbase Tesla Model Y L­ and­ noted that ­the­ middle-row­ chairs­ fold­ flat­ but­ don’t ­slide.­ While­ I wasn’t thrilled about having to make my way down the center aisle, airplane style, to get to the third row, I was impressed that the seatbacks in the second and third rows can be raised or lowered from the driver’s seat. Another neat trick is that if the front passenger’s seat is left too far back, it can adjust itself to prevent the middle row from crashing into it during folding. Also, the middle-row armrests automatically lowered when the door opened to make entry to the back easier. This is what I want from technology: smart seats. Now give me back a physical shifter.

Sparkle: At the end of the weekend, I asked the 11-year-old her thoughts on the Ranger. “It’s okay,” she said. “Only I like those cars where the tables fold out of the seats and the ceiling is all sparkly, like those caves where there are stars in the cave.” Rolls-Royces? I also like those cars. I respect her outlook, so I didn’t tell her what those cave stars actually are. Note to designers: Have you considered glowworms?

Like a sleeper agent activated late in the game, Elana Scherr didn’t know her calling at a young age. Like many girls, she planned to be a vet-astronaut-artist, and came closest to that last one by attending UCLA art school. She painted images of cars, but did not own one. Elana reluctantly got a driver’s license at age 21 and discovered that she not only loved cars and wanted to drive them, but that other people loved cars and wanted to read about them, which meant somebody had to write about them. Since receiving activation codes, Elana has written for numerous car magazines and websites, covering classics, car culture, technology, motorsports, and new-car reviews. In 2020, she received a Best Feature award from the Motor Press Guild for the C/D story "A Drive through Classic Americana in a Polestar 2."  In 2023, her Car and Driver feature story "In Washington, D.C.'s Secret Carpool Cabal, It's a Daily Slug Fest" was awarded 1st place in the 16th Annual National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards by the Los Angeles Press Club.

#4451. Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation

For decades, one of the most common recommendations for lowering high blood pressure has been simple: eat less salt. But a new scientific report suggests that this advice may be missing an equally important part of the equation.

Researchers say that increasing potassium intake, rather than focusing only on reducing sodium, could lead to better blood pressure control. By addressing both nutrients together, this approach could strengthen efforts to prevent hypertension and reduce the risk of serious cardiovascular problems.

The potential impact is enormous. High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, affects more than 1.28 billion adults worldwide and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, including heart attacks and strokes. Although public health recommendations have traditionally emphasized cutting sodium, researchers now argue that getting enough potassium deserves just as much attention.

Sodium and potassium are essential minerals that help regulate fluid balance, nerve signaling, and muscle function. Both also influence blood pressure, but they affect the body in different ways.

Eating too much sodium can cause the body to retain additional fluid, increasing the pressure inside blood vessels. Potassium helps counter some of sodium's effects by supporting the kidneys in removing excess sodium through urine. It also contributes to the normal functioning of blood vessel walls, which plays an important role in maintaining healthy blood pressure.

In a new report, physicians and health experts argue that dietary recommendations should address these two minerals together. Rather than treating sodium reduction as the primary solution, they propose combining it with greater potassium consumption to achieve stronger results.

"It is time to view dietary interventions holistically because food components interact and physiology is integrative across systems," said Naomi Fukagawa, M.D. Ph.D., professor of medicine emerita at the Robert Larner, M.D. College of Medicine at the University of Vermont and first author on the report. "Growing evidence shows that increasing dietary potassium as well as reducing sodium intake work together to better manage hypertension."

A Major Rethink of Blood Pressure Guidelines

The report, published in the peer-reviewed American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, was supported by the IAFNS Sodium in Food and Health Implications Committee.

The researchers examined the scientific evidence underlying current sodium and potassium recommendations, along with practical ways to reduce sodium consumption and increase potassium intake. They also explored the obstacles to implementing these changes and identified areas where additional research and updated public health policies could help improve outcomes.

One of the central concerns is that many people consume too much sodium while getting nowhere near enough potassium. Both dietary patterns can contribute to elevated blood pressure, making them important targets for prevention and treatment.

Despite widespread efforts to encourage people to limit salt, average sodium consumption continues to exceed recommended levels. Meanwhile, potassium intake remains "far below optimal levels in both developed and developing nations," according to the authors.

This imbalance suggests that focusing primarily on what people should eat less of may be overlooking an important opportunity to improve cardiovascular health by encouraging them to consume more of a beneficial nutrient.

Potassium is naturally present in many familiar foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, and dairy products. Bananas, potatoes, beans, leafy greens, and yogurt are examples of foods that can help increase potassium intake.

Another possibility is replacing some sodium chloride, the main ingredient in ordinary table salt, with potassium salts. These substitutes can help reduce sodium while simultaneously increasing potassium, potentially addressing both dietary goals at once.

However, creating these products presents challenges for food manufacturers. Adding too much potassium salt can produce an unpleasant metallic taste, limiting how much can be used without affecting flavor. Manufacturers must therefore find a balance that improves nutritional content while keeping foods appealing to consumers.

Increasing potassium is also not appropriate for everyone. People with kidney disease or those taking certain medications may have difficulty regulating potassium levels, so potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes should be used with medical guidance when these concerns apply.

A New Strategy for Fighting High Blood Pressure

The researchers emphasize that reducing sodium remains essential. Their proposal is not to abandon existing advice, but to expand it by recognizing that potassium intake is another major factor in blood pressure regulation.

The authors conclude that "dietary sodium reduction is a foundational strategy for hypertension prevention and management. However, new evidence supports a broadening of the current approach that focuses solely on sodium reduction and provides equal emphasis on increasing potassium intake."

For the more than one billion people living with hypertension, this shift in thinking could have significant implications. Instead of concentrating almost exclusively on reducing salt, future dietary recommendations may increasingly emphasize the combined benefits of consuming less sodium and more potassium.

The underlying message is straightforward: better blood pressure control may depend not only on what people remove from their diets, but also on what they add.

#4448. The Ratchet & Clank Game You Didn’t Know Existed is Shutting Down

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

I’ll admit, I have a tendency to hyperfixate on games and franchises that I care about, occasionally to the detriment of others. Even so, I like to consider myself sufficiently plugged-into this industry, especially when it comes to relatively big-name IPs like the Ratchet & Clank series. You can imagine my distinct confusion, then, when I heard today that Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble was shutting down, to which my response was, “what the heck is Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble?”

Apparently it is, soon to be “was,” a PvP live service shooter available for iOS and Android. The game saw a soft-launch in mid-2025 in limited territories like Canada, France, and parts of Asia, which probably explains why I have literally never heard of it alongside the fact that I don’t often pay much mind to mobile games in general.

In the wake of Destiny 2's upcoming final content update, thousands of of fans have called for Destiny 3 to begin development.

What’s especially interesting about this particular discontinuation, however, is that the game wasn’t even actually finished yet. That soft-launch was as far as the game had ever managed to get, with its planned global launch officially being scrapped and further development ceasing as of the game’s most recent update today, according to its official home page.

As the home page announcement explains, with the newest update pushed out today to mobile storefronts, no further updates for Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble will be released, and on November 21, the game will be pulled from said storefronts entirely.

This is a feature that looks at how live service games are dying as a popular choice in the industry.

For those who are still actively playing the game, you don’t have to stop playing it right away. While new players won’t be able to download the game from the Google Play or Apple App stores anymore following the delisting, anyone who already has the game downloaded will be able to keep playing multiplayer matches until the servers are officially closed in May 2027.

On November 21, the game will be pulled from storefronts entirely.

The game’s “Qwark Pass” seasons will continue running until the server closure, while the game’s “Super Pass” has been made free, with all of its related content now available to earn throughout the remaining seasons. Of course, said content will vanish into the ether once the game goes offline, so whether or not you can be bothered is up to you.

This also goes for any in-app purchases made on things like currency, cosmetics, upgrades, and so forth. If you’re looking to get a refund for any of that, the developers suggest you contact the Apple App Store and Google Play Store’s respective support lines to determine eligibility. Again, absolutely everything is being erased when the servers shutter in May, so whether you want a refund or to keep playing, you’d better act now.

In its final announcement, the developers offered some words of thanks to the players who joined them for the soft-launch process. “On behalf of the dev team and everyone helping to make the game, thanks to our amazing community for all your support, especially to those who have spent time playing, sharing feedback, and helping shape Ranger Rumble throughout its development,” they wrote.

While not as high-profile as some other historic live-service flops over the years, the discontinuation of Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble is another good sign that live-service games are reaching the end of an era. Aside from a very fortunate few that manage to keep attention with consistent updates and player-grabbing content like Fortnite’s One Piece event, the majority end up crashing and burning well before they can take off in earnest.

Sony in particular has been putting the kibosh on live-service games left and right for the last couple of years, mostly following the disastrous launch of Concord, and it seems even its major first-party PlayStation IPs like Ratchet & Clank aren’t safe from the proverbial axe.

Sony Interactive Entertainment executive Hideaki Nishino doubles down on multiplayer investments during a recent Famitsu interview.

#4446. Scientists discover a surprising clue to autism's origins hidden in the placenta

Scientists are still working to understand why autism develops. Genetics are known to play a major role, but researchers have also found that conditions during pregnancy can influence the likelihood of autism spectrum disorder.

A new study from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (CSHL) has uncovered a surprising connection between inflammation during pregnancy, changes in the placenta, and the development of autism-like traits in male mice. The findings suggest that certain developmental disruptions may begin much earlier than previously recognized, potentially offering new clues about autism's origins.

"To truly understand autism spectrum disorder, we have to look beyond the brain," CSHL Associate Professor Lucas Cheadle says. "Our work suggests that maternal immune activation and changes within the placenta are a gateway to autism for some unique individuals."

Scientists Identify an Early Window of Vulnerability

To investigate how inflammation affects fetal development, Cheadle and his colleagues triggered an immune response in pregnant mice at different stages of pregnancy. They used a substance that mimics the immune system's reaction to a viral infection without actually introducing a virus.

The researchers discovered that mouse fetuses were especially vulnerable when inflammation occurred 12.5 days into pregnancy. According to Irene Sanchez Martin, a postdoctoral researcher in Cheadle's laboratory, approximately one-third of the fetuses showed developmental abnormalities within just 24 hours.

Scientists have investigated the effects of maternal immune activation for decades, but these findings reveal signs of developmental disruption earlier than researchers had previously observed.

Even more striking was the difference between male and female fetuses. Across every experiment, autism-like traits appeared only in males, while females continued developing normally.

This unexpected distinction could provide insight into why autism is diagnosed substantially more often in boys than girls. What makes the finding especially intriguing is how early the difference appeared, before many of the biological changes normally associated with sex-specific development.

"It's really fascinating, because we're looking at an age which precedes hormonal surges. It precedes sexual differentiation in the brain and many other regions. So, it's surprising there would be a sex-based difference this early."

A Surprising Connection Between the Placenta and Autism

To determine why some developing mice were affected while others appeared protected, Cheadle and Sanchez Martin examined the placenta, the organ that connects a developing fetus to its mother and supports its growth throughout pregnancy.

Their attention centered on specialized cells called spongiotrophoblasts, which occupy a region of the mouse placenta where maternal and fetal cells interact.

In fetuses that developed normally, this part of the placenta remained healthy. However, male fetuses showing developmental abnormalities also had visible damage to these specialized cells.

Spongiotrophoblasts play an important role in helping the mother's immune system tolerate the developing fetus. This protection is essential because the fetus carries genetic material from both parents and is not genetically identical to the mother.

The researchers found that maternal immune activation could interfere with this protective function. When these placental cells become damaged, the mother's immune response may begin affecting the developing fetus in harmful ways.

Why Female Fetuses May Have a Hidden Advantage

The findings raise another intriguing question: Why were male fetuses vulnerable while females appeared unaffected?

One possibility is that male embryos produce distinctive proteins that can trigger an unfavorable maternal immune response following a viral infection. Another explanation is that female embryos possess some form of protection that helps them withstand inflammation during this sensitive developmental period.

Cheadle says, "A protective mechanism may exist within the female that could be harnessed to help the male. We're trying to understand how autism emerges in both sexes," he explains. "The evidence says that there are potentially different mechanisms."

These possibilities suggest that biological pathways involved in autism-like development may differ between males and females. Understanding those differences could help researchers identify why some individuals are more vulnerable to certain environmental influences during pregnancy.

Cheadle's team plans to investigate both male and female mice more closely to uncover the mechanisms responsible for these contrasting responses. Their work could eventually identify new targets for treatments and lead to strategies for intervening earlier in developmental processes associated with autism.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and do not establish that the same mechanisms cause autism in humans, they highlight an unexpected possibility: Important clues to autism's earliest development may lie not only in the brain, but also in the placenta and its interactions with the maternal immune system.

#4445. d4v41 and Jinggg leave Paper Rex after 7th–8th Champions finish, Pacific place secure

Paper Rex has parted with captain d4v41 and Jinggg, two Masters Toronto winners, after an early exit at Champions 2026. With its VCT Pacific partner place secure, the Singapore organisation is rebuilding by choice as free agency opens to every region.

Paper Rex has broken up the core of its VALORANT roster. The Singapore organisation is parting with its captain and one of its best-known players as the 2027 season approaches. d4v41 had been with Paper Rex since its founding in 2020. He played first on its CS:GO roster, then moved with the team to VALORANT. Jinggg joined on 28 September 2021.

Neither player has named a destination. In the farewell video Paper Rex released, d4v41 said he was moving to a new team. Jinggg wrote on X that he was excited about what comes next. d4v41 also asked fans to keep supporting the organisation after both have gone.

The split follows a season that faded at the end. Paper Rex were runners-up at both Masters Santiago and Masters London earlier in 2026. At Champions in Shanghai, they lost 2-0 to LOUD in the upper-bracket quarter-finals on 7 October. A 2-1 defeat to T1 in lower-bracket round one ended their run on 9 October. The event carried a $2,250,000 prize pool. LOUD went on to beat Team Vitality in the final.

The pair leave with a long record together. Jinggg helped Paper Rex to second place at Masters Copenhagen 2022. He was also part of the run to the Champions 2023 final, where the team were runners-up. Liquipedia lists both players in the line-up that won VCT 2025 Masters Toronto.

The changes are not forced by the league. The organisation is owned by IMPLS Entertainment Pte Ltd. Riot has cut the number of partner teams in each region from ten to eight for 2027–28. That leaves 32 across the four regions.

The Pacific format rewards that security. The eight partners receive seeded places at Kickoff in January 2027. Four further places go to teams that come through open qualifiers. Paper Rex can therefore reshape its roster without needing to qualify.

Two Masters winners on the open market could matter well beyond the Pacific. EMEA’s eight partners for 2027 are Fnatic, BBL Esports, FUT Esports, Team Heretics, Team Liquid, Gentle Mates, Karmine Corp and Team Vitality. Under Riot’s open qualifier rules, most regions require three of a team’s five players to come from that region. Teams must also keep three of five players between events to carry their progress forward. Those limits will frame how far any club can rebuild around new signings.

#4441. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult

Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

#4437. Jordan Esports Federation signs MoU with King Hussein Business Park to host more events

Priya Venkatesh has been following the money in esports since before brand deals were considered legitimate marketing. She got pulled into the scene through competitive fighting games and eventually found herself more interested in the contracts and partnerships behind the tournaments than the matches themselves. These days she focuses on how brands navigate esports sponsorships, where the smart money is going, and which deals are actually built to last versus the ones that look good in a press release.

The Jordan Esports Federation (JEF) has signed a memorandum of understanding with King Hussein Business Park (KHBP) in Amman, giving the national body a formal framework to stage more tournaments and events at the site it already calls home.

KHBP announced the deal on Sunday in a statement published on its website. Prince Omar bin Faisal, who is President of the JEF, attended the signing.

Under the MoU, the federation and the business park will jointly host and organise specialised competitions on the KHBP campus. They will also receive the international delegations and official guests that travel to those events. Beyond the competitive side, the two organisations plan to cooperate on media and marketing, look at shared education, training and community projects, and swap knowledge and expertise.

Neither party has disclosed financial terms or the length of the agreement.

KHBP CEO Eng. Ammar Ezzeddin presented the MoU as part of the park’s wider ambitions. “This partnership builds on our ongoing efforts to create an enabling environment for institutions, initiatives and high-potential sectors, and to establish KHBP as a hub for innovation and technology,” he said.

He added: “We look forward to helping the sector thrive and to hosting more tournaments and events that put Jordanian talent in the spotlight and raise the Kingdom’s profile in this field.”

JEF Vice President Hazem Bawab focused on the competitive and grassroots goals. “This partnership is a significant step in our drive to develop the esports industry in Jordan and elevate the standard of local, regional and international competitions and activities,” he said.

Bawab continued: “We look forward to drawing on the setup and capabilities that KHBP offers to scale our work, nurture young talent and launch joint programmes that help the industry grow and encourage greater participation.”

The deal formalises a relationship that already exists on the ground. According to The Esports Radar, the JEF, which is the government recognised regulator for esports in the country, is based at the park in West Amman.

A lot of that work happens at THE ARC, the arena and gaming dome inside the park. The same report lists past events there including the fourth Arab Esports League, a Women’s Esports Championship and Red Bull Login, which doubled as Jordan’s national final stage in Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2. The venue is also an incubation centre supported by the federation and the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship, and runs training camps for players hoping to turn professional.

KHBP has been a destination for esports investment for some time. In 2024, lounge operator True Gamers announced plans for an esports venue in Jordan at the business park, a project in which its CPO publicly thanked the JEF and Prince Omar.

The timing also puts Amman in the industry spotlight. PocketGamer.biz points out that Pocket Gamer Connects Jordan takes place on 7 and 8 November, bringing many of the region’s games industry stakeholders to the city later this week.

#4436. NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to reach a historic one-light-day milestone

Nearly 50 years after leaving Earth, NASA's Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone that will highlight just how far humanity's most distant spacecraft has traveled. But keeping the aging explorer operational has become an increasingly difficult challenge as its power supply slowly fades.

NASA engineers recently achieved two important developments in their effort to extend the mission. In September, they completed a complex energy conservation project designed to preserve the spacecraft's remaining scientific capabilities. Then, on October 20, Voyager 1 unexpectedly resumed communication with Earth after a mysterious 48-hour interruption.

NASA Engineers Find a Clever Way to Save Power

In early September, the Voyager team successfully replaced three devices aboard Voyager 1 with alternatives that consume less electricity. The carefully coordinated operation, nicknamed the "Big Bang," took months to prepare and was completed approximately six weeks after engineers carried out an identical procedure on Voyager 2.

The upgrade is expected to extend the operating lives of Voyager 1's remaining scientific instruments, allowing the spacecraft to continue collecting valuable information from interstellar space longer than previously expected.

Both Voyager spacecraft generate electricity using radioisotope thermoelectric generators. These systems produce electrical power from the heat released as plutonium undergoes radioactive decay. As that process continues, the spacecraft gradually lose generating capacity, with each probe experiencing a decline of approximately 4 watts annually.

After almost five decades in space, that steady loss has left engineers with very little power to spare. To keep the missions operating, NASA has progressively shut down equipment that is no longer essential.

The Big Bang presented an especially difficult engineering challenge because all three replacements had to happen simultaneously. The six devices involved help maintain temperatures inside the spacecraft despite the extreme cold of space. Replacing the three original devices together was necessary to reduce electricity consumption while preserving the proper distribution of heat throughout Voyager 1.

Keeping Voyager 1's Science Mission Alive

Power limitations have already forced NASA to deactivate two of Voyager 1's scientific instruments in recent years. When the spacecraft launched in 1977, it carried 10 instruments dedicated to scientific research. Several were shut down after Voyager completed its encounters with the outer planets, while others remained active to investigate increasingly distant regions of space.

Among the areas studied was the outer heliosphere, the enormous region of particles and magnetic fields produced by the Sun. Both Voyager spacecraft have since crossed beyond this boundary into interstellar space, making them the only spacecraft ever to directly examine the environment outside the Sun's heliosphere.

Preserving their remaining instruments is particularly important because no other missions can currently collect measurements from this distant region. Without the Big Bang upgrade, NASA would have faced the possibility of shutting down another Voyager 1 instrument as early as summer 2027.

Mysterious Communication Loss Raises New Questions

Even with the successful power conservation effort, Voyager 1 continues to encounter unexpected problems.

NASA temporarily lost contact with the spacecraft on October 18 and 19, when the agency's Deep Space Network failed to receive its radio signal during two scheduled communication attempts separated by 24 hours.

The network consists of large radio antennas at three locations around the world, allowing NASA to exchange signals with spacecraft exploring the Moon and more distant destinations. At the time of the interruption, Voyager 1 was approximately 16 billion miles (24 billion kilometers) from Earth.

After two unsuccessful attempts to detect the spacecraft, its signal unexpectedly returned on October 20, roughly 48 hours after the interruption began. Communication has remained established since then, and engineers subsequently sent commands to investigate the problem.

NASA has not yet determined exactly what caused the incident. However, engineers discovered that one set of Voyager 1's thrusters had stopped operating and that the spacecraft had automatically activated its backup thrusters.

This behavior is part of a built-in safety system known as fault protection. When the onboard computers recognize a potential problem with active equipment, they can switch to backup hardware, place the spacecraft into a stable configuration, and suspend normal activities. This gives controllers on Earth an opportunity to investigate and determine the appropriate response.

"This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," said Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "We're relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened."

Voyager 1 Approaches a Historic One-Light-Day Milestone

While NASA continues investigating the communication interruption, Voyager 1 is moving toward another remarkable achievement.

Traveling through interstellar space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), the spacecraft is expected to reach a distance of 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth on November 18. That distance equals one light-day, meaning it takes light an entire 24 hours to travel between Earth and the probe.

No other human-made object has ever reached such a distance.

The milestone also illustrates the extraordinary challenges of communicating with a spacecraft so far from home. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, so commands transmitted from Earth will require a full day to reach Voyager 1. Any response sent back will take another 24 hours, creating a total communication delay of 48 hours.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL.

Crossing the one-light-day threshold will not produce any physical change in Voyager 1 or its surroundings. The spacecraft will continue traveling through the same interstellar environment, unaware that it has passed a milestone of special significance to people on Earth.

Instead, the achievement serves as a powerful reminder of the enormous distances separating objects in the universe and the remarkable endurance of a spacecraft launched nearly half a century ago. Despite fading power, aging equipment, and unexpected technical problems, Voyager 1 continues its historic journey farther from Earth than any other human-made object.

It’s pretty clear at this stage that Arc Raiders is one of the biggest launches of 2025. More interesting than the numbers themselves, however, is that this is an extraction shooter - a subgenre which has typically been thought of as niche.

If you’ve been paying the PvPvE game any attention, you could easily see how (and why) it keeps breaking its own records.

Today, publisher Nexon announced in a press release (via Gematsu) that Arc Raiders has now sold over 4 million copies. The game came out on October 30, which means it managed to sell that many copies in a little over 10 days.

The news comes on the same day that developer Embark Studios announced that the game had more than 700,000 concurrent players across all platforms over the weekend. Over the same weekend on Steam alone, Arc Raiders broke its own Steam concurrent record with a new peak of 462,488 players - which is a significant chunk of that 700,000+ player base.

This marks the second time the extraction shooter has broken its own concurrent player records, which is something very few games have managed in the past. Arc Raiders remains a top-seller, too. On Steam, it’s currently the second-best seller globally (by revenue), sitting just below Counter-Strike 2.

“The many different ways you play and participate in ARC Raiders have completely blown us away, going far beyond what we ever imagined. You surprise us, you outsmart us, and you keep us on our toes. We wouldn’t have it any other way,” the developer wrote on Twitter.

Embark recently published a roadmap to highlight all the new content coming to the game over the remainder of this year. The first new map is set to arrive this month alongside new Arc units, new gameplay items, new events and more.

Just over the weekend, the game received several new Map Conditions that completely alter the way they play. The developer has already rolled out a couple of updates since launch, in order to tackle exploits and fix a few launchday bugs.

KRÜ took the long route. They beat Gen.G GC 2-1 in the upper-bracket quarter-finals on 23 October. A 2-0 loss to Shopify Rebellion Gold on 27 October then dropped them into the lower bracket. Gentle Mates fought back, but KRÜ closed it out 14-12 in overtime. Gentle Mates then won Split 13-8 to force a decider. KRÜ led 11-5 on Ascent and won it by the same margin as Split.

KRÜ’s own record at the event had improved steadily. They finished 7th–8th in 2022 and 5th–6th in each of the next two years. Last year they came fourth.

For European fans, it was a painful near miss. Gentle Mates GC arrived as EMEA’s top seed on circuit points. The team had not lost a series in São Paulo before the final, according to Esports News UK.

It capped a strong debut season in the circuit. Gentle Mates won EMEA Stage 1 by sweeping G2 Gozen 3-0 on 22 February. They lost the Stage 2 final to SK Nebula on 24 May without winning a map. On 30 August they lost the Stage 3 final to G2 Gozen in a fifth map. Silver in São Paulo leaves them with one title from four finals this year.
