#4387. Remedy Explains Control Resonant's Most Memorable, Unexpected Sequence And Its [REDACTED] Inspirations

Please allow the first sentence here to warn you that this interview discusses a portion of Control Resonant that takes place near the end of the game and is arguably the most unexpected and surprising sequence. I encourage you to experience it without spoilers. So if you haven't beaten the game yet, please do, and then come back to this page.However, if you have beaten the game, or curiosity has driven you to learn what game has been redacted from the headline and why (it's the 1995 Super Nintendo RPG, EarthBound, by the way), then please read on.

In the late-game of Control Resonant – basically right before you tackle the final confrontation – the game suddenly shifts timeframe and genre to become a 16-bit RPG. The nostalgic lens turns the game into something that feels like 1995's EarthBound, complete with turn-based battles, in order to explain the trauma that Jesse and Dylan went through at a young age after they came across an object of power: the slide projector. The whole sequence is funny, heartbreaking, weird, and importantly effective at making you feel you are seeing a part of their past. It was particularly effective on me as I have fond memories of playing EarthBound and games like it when I was young. To see and experience Dylan and Jesse's childhood this way felt accurate, as absurd as that sounds.

I reached out to Remedy to specifically discuss that portion of the game. You can find the full e-mail interview below with the team members who contributed to its creation.

The big RPG backstory sequence for Jesse and Dylan – why approach the storytelling that way?

Lead level designer, Anne-Marie Grönroos: The basis for the whole sequence is that the Hedron attacks Dylan's mind, breaks his reality apart, and he has to rebuild himself. We wanted the reality-breaking part to affect the game itself and have the player feel some of the confusion Dylan is feeling by breaking the fourth wall.

Who pitched that sequence, how did they pitch it, and was it difficult to sell to the larger team?

Grönroos: At Remedy, ideas rarely come from a single person or team, and we rarely do formal pitches, but rather discuss and workshop ideas cross-craft until they start taking the shape of something we like. The initial idea from the writer was for this to be a text-based adventure, to return to a very early form of a video game to show that the Patterning is devolving him, but an Alan Wake 2 DLC had already done that, and we wanted to find something else.

Independently, some months ago a level designer had suggested a sidequest with JRPG pixel graphics, but that had gone nowhere. I remembered that and suggested doing an old Final Fantasy-style JRPG here, which also felt more fitting since that’s the type of game Dylan and Jesse would have played in their childhood, and not a text-based adventure. People got excited about that, and after some concerns about feasibility, we went forth with it. It helped that the level designer who had originally wanted to do the JRPG side quest is a big fan of these types of games and has made them before. I wouldn’t have dropped something this crazy on someone who wasn’t passionate about it and ready to figure out how to do it with our engine that’s not built for anything like this.

Is EarthBound (Mother in Japan) the primary inspiration for that sequence? Are there big fans of those games at Remedy?

Senior level designer in charge of the JRPG quest, Arhi Makkonen:The whole Quest was born from that childhood feeling I had when playing old JRPGs – Final Fantasy, Breath of Fire, Chrono Trigger, Secret of Mana, Bahamut Lagoon, and yes, Mother. The most important thing for me was capturing that feeling of a time when games felt like magic. I think many people can relate to that nostalgia, and now Jesse and Dylan share that feeling in the game.Visually, Mother was a major inspiration of course. Juuso Anttila is the concept artist who did all the splendid pixel art for Rebuild quest. Mother's style fits the mysterious Americana small town vibe perfectly. We also couldn't pass up the pun about a story revolving around "Not-Mother" that was made in the style of Mother.

Was it difficult to implement the sequence into the game? Did Remedy's Northlight Engine need significant work to account for the sequence?

Makkonen: The Northlight engine was designed to work perfectly for third-person action games. Well, Rebuild Quest is pretty much the opposite of that. Northlight is a specialized tool rather than a general-purpose one, so we had to come up with some rather creative solutions to create a 2D JRPG.

First of all, we’re faking the 2D look. In reality, the entire JRPG Ordinary exists within a 3D world that the camera simply views from directly overhead. It occupies a tiny patch in a remote corner of the game world—a space where 3D Dylan would barely have room to stand. The entire game-within-a-game is written in Lua; our incredibly versatile game designer, Tommi Saalasti, created the underlying system, upon which I was then able to build the story.

Since we didn't really have the tools to create a game like this, I had to hand-code every single detail. Dylan takes one step up, Dylan turns left (where Jesse hopefully is at that moment), text box 1, text box 2. The Lua script for the Rebuild quest alone probably contains as many lines of code as all the other quests in the game combined. And then there were things like animations were restricted to a maximum of two frames, and some UI elements were created using static particle effects.

So yes, we faced all sorts of challenges and compromises, but at the heart of it all was a wonderful story – simply told in a somewhat unconventional way. We trusted that the narrative would make up for some of the imperfections.

Remedy has a reputation for big unexpected and often crazy singular moments. What are the conversations like around delivering those? In pre-production, are there conversations like, "What is the big moment for this one?" Or do they happen pretty naturally?

Grönroos: They both happen naturally and we also have conversations about what the big moments should be. Sometimes we like a section so much that we decide to put even more resources and importance to it, even if it wasn’t supposed to be all that important from the get-go. The Into the Sinkhole quest, for instance, is a quest that wasn’t planned to be a “tentpole moment” from the start, but we kept putting more effort into it when it was shaping up to be something very special.

But most setpieces in the game were planned to be such from the early stages of pre-production. In Resonant, we wanted to have multiple standout moments instead of a single sequence like the Ashtray Maze overshadowing everything else, and I’m happy to see that players have different favorites.

And a different approach from Control is that several of these memorable moments (Sinkhole, Underpass Fault, the JRPG section) are more emotional and subdued instead of bombastic action (although we also have big action setpieces), which was an interesting challenge itself.

Was there a fear that the visuals would limit the emotional impact of the sequence?

Grönroos: Yes, but we decided to trust the writing. Several other games have managed to deliver a similar emotional impact despite pixel graphics (and sometimes because of them, since the level [of] abstraction can make characters more relatable and up to the player’s interpretation), so we weren’t too concerned.

Was there a fear that action game fans would be frustrated by the RPG sequence?

Grönroos: Yes, this was the main concern about the sequence. It was a very polarizing sequence in the playtests: people either loved or hated it. We did discuss shortening it significantly, but in the end decided to keep it as it is but added some fast travel options and make some parts skippable. There were more fans than haters, and we didn’t want to sacrifice something we really enjoyed.

How concerned were you about the actual RPG mechanics of that sequence?

Makkonen: Since Rebuild doesn't feature a vast number of battles, we didn't need to build particularly deep RPG or progression systems. The combat served as an additional storytelling tool – illustrating how bullies torment Dylan, showing his first fight (against rats, naturally), and depicting his eventual abduction by the FBC.

Refining the combat to be simple, yet offer the player meaningful choices required a few iterations. In addition to standard attacks, the children can occasionally use special abilities: Dylan delivers a heavy blow to a single enemy, while Jesse fires at everyone. Enemies deal enough damage that defending becomes necessary when multiple foes target the same character.

The lightbulbs in The Underpass mission goes in similarly unexpected, animated directions. How did that mission come about? What was the pitch like for that one?

Grönroos: That one started with the idea of doing something comically mundane, switching lightbulbs, and adding a paranatural twist to it. The cartoon man wasn’t in the initial version, but instead we were going to do live action videos and have Dylan get stuck in that video as the end twist. They were supposed to be old-fashioned “work safety” videos explaining how to change lightbulbs, and as the quest went on, it became more and more obvious that the maintenance guy in the videos was too aware of what Dylan was doing. This all came out from a one-hour workshop.

There wasn’t really a pitch, but rather a back-and-forth like “could we do a quest about Dylan changing lightbulbs in a ritualistic way? We could have these sentient work safety videos explain how to do it and “Dylan could get trapped inside the video.” Much later, when the live action turned out to be a no-go, we pivoted to the current cartoon instead, and that was even funnier than our initial idea.

#4386. 7 Video Games That Could Sweep in The Game Awards, Ranked

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Winter holidays bring joy through family gatherings and discounted video games, but they have also become synonymous with awards ceremonies celebrating the year's finest releases.

In the case at hand, 2026 has established itself as a magnificent trip around the sun thanks to the numerous masterful titles that have been, or will be, released during its 12 months, making for a fiercely contested race to see which is the best.

The number of events held for this purpose is as vast as it is diverse, although all eyes are on December 10th, the day the interactive industry's Ballon d'Or is awarded.

Therefore, if you're as eager as I am to see if any video game can come close to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's phenomenal success last year, I recommend you read this list of seven video games that could sweep The Game Awards, ranked.

The first and most underrated video game to appear on this list is none other than Big Walk, a game that will arrive completely silent despite having the power to surprise more than a few on this special night.

That it will win Best Multiplayer should be a given, but this would be merely the bare minimum of the recognition that House House's team has earned through one of the most special and creative indie games of recent years.

Because of this, and considering it's this year's highest-rated game on Metacritic if we don't count remasters and remakes, there's more than enough reason to believe it could become 2026's most acclaimed independent production.

My bets for Game Direction and Audio Design are bolder, especially since these are usually awarded to larger projects with bigger budgets. However, given what happened last year, I wouldn't rule out Big Walk silencing more than a few detractors.

This article ranks the Game of the Year nominee classes from The Game Awards each year of the 2020s.

A particularly curious case is that of Control Resonant, which presents itself as a solid piece in numerous departments, even though I don't believe its overall acclaim is sufficient to be a Game of the Year contender.

Said detail aside, Remedy knows what it's like to have a string of successes after Alan Wake 2 won three of its eight nominations in 2023, and its latest project could repeat that feat with even greater force.

Specifically, in terms of the audiovisual component, it's by far one of the year's strongest contenders, which hasn't stood out for its narratives or art direction at Control Resonant's level, except in the indie scene.

That a title can win so many awards without being Game of the Year already happened in 2022 with God of War: Ragnarök, and for reasons very similar to those experienced by Kratos's latest adventure, I think we could be facing the same scenario now.

Capcom has been, arguably by a wide margin, the most outstanding developer of the year, having released Monster Hunter Stories 3, Pragmata, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, and, most relevantly for this occasion, Resident Evil: Requiem.

Angela Sant'Albano's stellar performance as Grace Ashcroft already guarantees a strong chance of winning an award despite the fierce competition, as does its status as the best horror game of the year and all that entails in terms of gameplay and audio design.

From there, Resident Evil: Requiem faces an uphill battle to win all the awards for which it will surely be a candidate, as it is undeniably one of the best games of the year.

Will being the best Resident Evil be enough to secure every possible nomination? Time will tell, but its candidacy and the seriousness with which it must be approached can be anticipated from this very moment.

The Game Awards has six awesome titles up for Game Of The Year in 2025, but here are seven more that still feel like they've been snubbed.

The Game Awards' biggest winners last year ranged from indie to AA titles, opening up a world of possibilities for this and future iterations, especially for extraordinary adventures like Mina the Hollower.

The current lineup isn't as fertile for indie products to take center stage as it did in 2025, but I'm certain that, if any prospect can truly achieve that, it's Yacht Club Games' masterpiece.

As for Best Indie Game, Best Action-Adventure Game, and Game Direction, I'd bet my life that this wonderful ode to classic video games will be in the running, aiming to take home those awards, though it's outstanding enough in the other categories to warrant consideration as well.

The interactive medium's pendulum is increasingly swinging in favor of indie games in these turbulent times, where the biggest companies keep making bad decisions, so Mina the Hollower could capitalize on those protest votes.

The year's not-so-surprise surprise is Phantom Blade Zero, which stands on the shoulders of Black Myth: Wukong to likely become the Chinese video game with the most nominations and prizes at The Game Awards.

As part of the top three contenders for the People's Choice Award, I see S-Game's gem as a work robust enough to compete with the two titans that you and I both know round out this list, which says everything you need to know about its quality.

Its greatest strength is its unique character, stemming from a singular design, composition, and presentation philosophy that we've seen only a handful of times, allowing it to stand out with literally unparalleled ease and fluidity among the rest.

It has more than enough quality to win any title it's given, so much so that, if we were in any other year of the decade, I could easily predict that Phantom Blade Zero would be GOTY.

The Best Games For Impact Nominees Of All Time are emotional and thought-provoking experiences.

Nevertheless, the year is 2026, and it just so happens that it coincides with the return of what many consider the best video game of all time, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake.

If there's one reason why I feel most action-adventure games will have a tough time, it's because the quintessential adventure has returned, the one that paved the way for the entire genre in the three decades following its release.

From the music to its underrated art direction, including its technical and gameplay splendor, it's safe to say that the Ocarina of Time remake will be present even in the Muppet segments created by the legendary Geoff Keighley.

In 1998, there was no The Game Awards to give Link's odyssey the recognition it deserved, so don't be surprised if the video game industry, as a whole, makes this year the perfect moment to rectify that omission.

If we take into account what its immediate predecessor did and what its creators have promised to do with it, there's no doubt that the top contender to sweep The Game Awards is Grand Theft Auto 6.

Rockstar is fully aware that, every year they release a game, December becomes a month of metaphorical and material praise, given their habit of releasing the most ambitious and massive titles the industry is ready to see.

Link is a formidable competitor, and that's indisputable, yet Lucia and Jason have the added momentum of being the most anticipated video game in history and the most expensive ever made, making them immediate candidates for a third of the event's categories.

It's difficult to predict with certainty, though if there's one thing I can be partially sure of, it's that Ocarina of Time and GTA 6 will quickly make this article obsolete by taking home practically every award between them.

These titles were left at the gates of glory, but they deserved to be called Game of the Year.

#4383. Crusaders Heaven tier list of every skin in the game

A detailed tier list of normal and exclusive skins in Crusader Heaven ranked by their effectiveness.

Crusaders Heaven is one of the best Roblox combat games based on JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure. As you play, you'll see that the exciting skins, trading system, and accessories make Crusaders Heaven interesting not only for JoJo fans but also for those who like collectables. In this article, you will find every in-game skin sorted into an impressive Crusaders Heaven tier list.

It includes normal skins available at the time of writing and limited exclusives that can be obtained only during a specific time. The tier list might come in handy not only for beginners but also for experienced players who want to expand their knowledge about Crusaders Heaven.

WHAT IS OUR CRUSADERS HEAVEN TIER LIST? The game has a comprehensive skins system, and our Crusaders Heaven tier list includes a particular Extra Tier for event-exclusive skins. They can't be obtained nowadays but are still worth a unique place in this guide.

Tier SS includes the rarest skins in Crusaders Heaven. These are a great way to stand out among other players and look completely unique. The only issue is that Tier SS skins are the rarest in Crusaders Heaven, so you might just end up spending a lot of time trying to get them.

The World: OVA The World: OVA is the most exciting skin you can get for The World stand, the main stand of Dio Brando. It's a strong stand that's most effective at close range. Using The World with OVA skin is the best way to make your character look more appealing.

Tier S still includes valuable skins. Even though getting them is a little bit more straightforward than tier SS skins, they are hard to get if you're not spending real money on the game.

Star Platinum Television Star Platinum Television is the skin for one of the most potent stands in Crusaders Heaven. Even though it only features visual improvements for your character, using Television Skin for your Star Platinum is one of the best ways to stand out among all players.

Tier A skins are way more accessible than tier SS/S skins. Using tier A skins is a great option if you want to look cool and don’t want to donate money or spend dozens of hours trying to obtain the best ones.

Star Platinum: The Galaxy The Galaxy is another skin for Star Platinum stand in Crusaders Heaven. Even though this skin is less rare than Star Platinum Television, many players still like to opt for The Galaxy instead of Television.

Tier B includes valuable skins that can be used even during later game stages. They are perfectly suitable for trading in order to get more expensive skins, as well as for wearing them just to look cool. You should never underestimate tier B skins in Crusaders Heaven.

Diego Diego, or Diego Brando, is an outfit of one of the secondary antagonists in Crusaders Heaven. Even though this skin seems pretty valuable, it belongs to Tier B. So, getting it is not a big problem even if you are a beginner.

Tier C includes the most accessible skins in Crusaders Heaven. Even though experienced players don't really appreciate outfits from tier C, they are still widely used among beginners. And if you're not a big fan, remember you can use tier C skins to trade for a better outfit.

Shiny King Crimson Shiny King Crimson is one of the most accessible skins for the King Crimson stand. It is a human-looking stand that appears slightly bigger than your character in Crusaders Heaven.

Tier E is the last tier and includes the worst skins in Crusaders Heaven. These skins have no value, which isn't surprising since most tier E skins are based on the appearance of minor characters from JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure.

Shiny Killer Queen Shiny Killer Queen is a copy of Shiny King Crimson, but for the Killer Queen stand of Kira Yoshikage in Crusaders Heaven. The only difference is that Shiny Killer Queen is more accessible, which is why it's in tier E.

The Event tier includes exclusive event stand skins that are available only during a specific time of the year. Sometimes, Event tier skins are more difficult to obtain than those in tier SS. So if you have one, you're sure to stand out from the crowd if you wear the exclusive skins from this tier.

Valentine Platinum Valentine Platinum is considered the most valuable skin for the Star Platinum stand, which will make you look unique even when compared to players with tier SS skins. The only issue is that it is nearly impossible to get Valentine Platinum nowadays.

And that's our Crusaders Heaven tier list! Keep in mind that this article is regularly updated. It always includes skins from the latest Crusaders Heaven updates, so feel free to share it with friends.

#4382. The latest Arc Raiders patch is almost entirely about fixing exploits, including all the clipping through locked rooms business

Embark is clearly sick of Arc Raiders players exploiting the game's mechanics to push each other around, and clip through doors and walls.

A fresh Arc Raiders patch has arrived, bringing a host of new fixes to several exploits players have recently been relying on to do things they’re not supposed to, and bypass certain mechanics to get into areas without having to go through proper channels.

The patch is fairly small, and surprisingly doesn’t include any buffs or nerfs to anything in particular.

The list of notes for update 1.4.0 is compact, with a clear focus on addressing several exploits. The biggest one, of course, is the addition of “exploit mitigation mechanisms” to stop players from glitching through locked doors.

This fix applies to all maps, and it’s intended to address an issue whereby players would not bring the required keys to access those areas of the various maps. Locked rooms, if they can be unlocked, often hide a wealth of high-tier and rare loot.

But players have also been using similar exploits to clip through walls and access areas outside the playspace, allowing them to ambush enemy players and set up traps that would be impossible for others to detect.

The game’s recent patch, which was released exactly one week ago, mainly consisted of balance tweaks to some of the more popular weapons and mines. However, it also introduced a few fixes to prevent players from clipping through walls by using barricades.

While on the subject of being in places where you’re not supposed to, the patch blocked exterior access to the locked room inside Spaceport's Control Tower, making it only accessible from inside the tower.

1.4.0 also fixes an especially nasty exploit that allowed players to bring up their weapons much faster than normal by quickly swapping to the quick use menu. There’s a range of smaller fixes for lighting and texture bugs here, too, and you can read all about it in the full change log below:

#4379. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 23, 2026

This week has been home to some disheartening news. BioWare, the creators of games like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, is being shut down amid a flurry of layoffs. It's another frustrating story from a struggling video game industry. Below you will find some of our stories about the legendary developer, including our massive 2016 oral history. And then after that, you can read about our recommendations of what to play this weekend.

I spent the early hours playing Final Fantasy Resonance trying to figure out precisely why I couldn't put it down. I eventually realized that the game manages in a very purposeful way to answer that quiet need I've so frequently had: "I wish I could experience a game just like Final Fantasy IV or VI again, for the first time, but with a new cast and story." That's pretty much what you can expect here; Resonance is a very purposeful throwback experience that harkens to the early days of FF pixel adventures, but with several modern conveniences, graphical flourishes, and depth added into the mix. It's a big and refreshingly wholesome journey of entertaining party members, summoning giant creatures, flying an airship across the world, and fighting turn-based battles that include absurd spell effects. It's one of my favorite games of the year, and well worth the time it will take to explore. Read our full review for more.

Expect to hear a lot of people proclaiming this as "one of the good ones," as Modern Warfare came out swinging this week with a strong campaign, compelling additions to competitive multiplayer, and an impressive extraction shooter mode in the form of DMZ. I've already been impressed by the first few hours of the campaign, which offers a tense, harrowing, and often disturbingly brutal story that bounces between a number of character perspectives. The gunplay feels tuned in, the traversal and melee is satisfying, and the narrative beats grounded in excellent actin performances. Our reviewer has spent even more time with the full game, and can share their full perspective to help inform whether you want to take a dive into this year's installment.

The Nintendo Sports franchise, which began with Wii Sports in 2006, has never been about the single-player experience. That remains true 20 years later in Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. But this time around, Nintendo has boosted the amount of content beyond what the series has typically provided, appealing to all player counts, all while retaining its trademark approachability. Whether you're joining together with three friends for some friendly competition across the package's 12 sports or you're trying to climb the Island Crown ladder by beating increasingly difficult single-player opponents, Switch Sports Resort is a great motion-controlled collection.

Halloween is around the corner. As you’re buying overpriced candy, deciding which version of the Joker to dress up as, and debating between watching Obsession and Backrooms over a cup of cider, it’s the perfect time to replay old horror games or dive into new ones. 2026 has a solid roster of choices for the latter thanks to releases like Resident Evil Requiem, Paranormasight: The Mermaid’s Curse, and Silent Hill: Townfall, but Tenebris Somnia shouldn’t be overlooked if you’re looking for a cool indie throwback.

Part retro-inspired adventure game, part live-action indie horror film, you’ll uncover the mystery of a nightmare-induced apartment building and battle horrors to rescue your trapped ex. The gameplay is survival horror 101, but it’s executed well, with consistently clever and inventive puzzle-solving as a highlight. It may not be a graphical powerhouse, but Tenebris Somnia still maintains a creepy atmosphere thanks to solid scares partly delivered by effective and well-made live-action cinematics. If you’re going to binge horror films, you may as well play one too. You can read my full review here.

Full disclosure: I have not played One Piece: Grand Gourmet. I was trying to finish up Castlevania: Belmont's Curse when a review game landed in my lap that I've had to give my full attention. That said, I have watched a lot of the One Piece anime, have a cat named Nami, and dog named Luffy.

I don't know if One Piece: Grand Gourmet is any good, but I like the premise and pixel graphics. One Piece is a very malleable franchise (which is why its live action adaptation is pretty good), so the idea of managing a restaurant as Sanji feels like it could be a very good fit. I plan on climbing aboard with all my hopes and dreams soon. And it is out now, which is good to know.

Similar to the entry above, I have not yet played Stupid Never Dies yet (there are too many video games!), but we like to use this weekly article to call out the new video games of the week. I am eager to check out Stupid Never Dies primarily because of its pop-punk soundtrack and 2000s aesthetic. I think it has the potential to be a fun, nostalgic throwback to my youth when I was learning Blink-182's "Dammit" on guitar and playing Devil May Cry.

The Blood of Dawnwalker has been out for just over seven weeks now, but I wouldn't blame you if you haven't finished it – or even started it – yet. A lot has come out! But if you need a reason to jump back in, this week's 1.1 update is a great excuse – the devs have added hundreds of bug fixes and other minor improvements, so it should run better than it ever did before. There's also an even easier difficulty mode if you want to cruise through without worrying about combat, and a new in-game potion that lets you respec all your skill points. I stalled out about halfway through (when I started playing Wolverine), but I'm planning to jump back in this weekend.

Oh, and you can pet dogs and cats now. Maybe I should have led with that.

Multiplayer physics mountain-climbing game Peak became one of the most viral co-op experiences of 2025 (I refuse to use the term friendslop), but only PC players have enjoyed its wacky shenanigans. That changed this week as Peak is now available on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and Switch 2. Either alone or, preferably, alongside up to three friends, you’ll try to ascend procedurally generated, absurdly unrealistic mountains riddled with dangers. Working together is key, a tricky prospect thanks to the in-game proximity chat that necessitates sticking together, but griefing each other, intentionally or otherwise, is just as entertaining – maddeningly frustrating at times, but entertaining. Peak on consoles includes all post-launch content and, best of all, supports crossplay for all platforms.

The original Azul remains one of my all-time favorite games even after many years, but it just misses the bar with its strategic complexity to be one I'd pull out to play with the kids. That why I was especially delighted to find that Azul Kids is one of those rare "adapted for children" projects that turned out extremely well.

Players take on the roll of creative young artists building mosaic displays with various colored tiles. The concept remains simple enough to work for even very young players of age five or six, but the whole family should have fun with the approachable strategy implications of choosing tiles and completing your masterpiece.

#4378. Sony Launches New Offensive in the Console Exclusive Wars

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

In the modern games industry, it feels like the lines between consoles and PC have been constantly blurred, both by internal decisions to port games and by the rising cost of consoles themselves. More and more players are hopping to PC, and each of the big three console providers has come to different conclusions on how to address this challenge.

While some JRPGs disappear, others return from oblivion after years without new releases.

After years of being rather wishy-washy with the status of its first-party titles, Sony is leaning hard back into exclusivity, marked by a new PlayStation Exclusive banner noted by a user on Twitter. This seems like a major PR step for Sony’s new effort to keep their exclusives truly exclusive, with no plans for major first-party releases like Ghosts of Yotei and Until Dawn 2 to bridge the gap to PC.

The latest console generation has been rough for everybody other than Nintendo, whose tried-and-true strategy of providing simple, exclusive hardware has been keeping food on the table since the company’s founding, with a notable hiccup during the Wii U era. After years of attempting to mirror XBOX’s focus on making a multi-platform space, it seems that Sony is leaning back on old tactics.

Sony’s exclusives have been an important part of keeping the PlayStation relevant, and their willingness to port early PS5 exclusives to PC made it much easier for many to ignore the high-priced console, a mistake they’re looking to rectify. With the inclusion of a special decal on various recent and upcoming PlayStation exclusives, it really does seem like Sony is done letting its heavy hitters float off the reservation.

More and more players are hopping to PC, and each of the big three console providers has come to different conclusions on how to address this challenge.

This makes XBOX the last console willing to port its exclusives to PC, a move that keeps Microsoft’s choice as the hardest to purchase by far. Consoles need some kind of major selling point to get consumers on their side, and exclusives are the easiest way of convincing many to play ball. After recent game shutdowns and studio layoffs, it’s become clear Sony needs to shake something up.

Leaning back on exclusives sucks for PC players, but makes sense for the general health of PlayStation as a platform. Rising console costs have made the choice between console and PC a much closer debate, and allowing games to hop onto Steam or Epic just shifts the scale even harder in PC’s favor. From here on, Sony should be able to earn back their strongest argument, especially with heavy hitters like God of War: Laufey coming in Q1 of 2027.

This most recent console generation has made it clear that decent power and ease of use isn’t enough to keep a console platform viable, as both XBOX and PlayStation have struggled immensely. The Switch 2, on the other hand, has been a huge success for Nintendo, largely thanks to the incredible quality of titles that only Nintendo’s machine can play.

It feels a bit like a no-brainer, but it really does come down to the games on offer for many, and if your machine is willing to let those games go to PC, why shouldn’t players nab a PC instead? Consoles will never be able to match the sheer features and flexibility of PC, so their greatest arguments will always come in the form of exclusive titles, a lesson Sony is finally remembering.

Even XBOX is growing a bit more heavy-handed with where exactly its first-party titles go, but keeping the door open to PC might come back to bite them more than the extra copies sold help. We’re approaching the tail end of this console generation, forcing PlayStation and XBOX both to make some major moves. The only question is who will come out on top of this decades-old rivalry.

#4376. Phantom Blade Zero Review In Progress – Shaping Up To Be One Of The Best Action Games I've Ever Played

Phantom Blade Zero is an astounding achievement for the action genre. So astounding that I feel pulled to experience everything it has to offer… and that means instead of rolling credits, I’ve been busy completing story-critical side quests and more to get the most complete ending. That’s another way of saying I am enjoying this game very, very much but still need more time to render a final verdict, which is why you’re reading a review-in-progress of Phantom Blade Zero rather than a scored piece.

Though I’m not interested in guesstimating a score right now, I know it will be high because Phantom Blade Zero impresses and then some. It is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, and I’m shocked to be writing that. This is a debut of sorts for developer S-Game, which has dabbled in mobile games and smaller-scale titles; it’s the team’s first triple-A release, and its first game of this kind. This studio is so clearly a dedicated student of the genre, analyzing what works here and what works there in other action greats to create something of its own. It looks forward at what action games can do, can play like, can look like, while looking back at the games before it and understanding why those games – games like Devil May Cry, Elden Ring, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Bayonetta, and just about every other quality action game you can think of – continue to be ones we hold so highly. Should it stick the landing, Phantom Blade Zero will join that echelon of action pedigree.

Protagonist Soul is a quiet, mostly stoic martial arts master who prefers to let his blades (of which there are so, so many) do the talking. The Order he’s sworn his life to betrays him, and, in an effort to right wrongs, he discovers a villainous conspiracy to seize full power of the blood-soaked Chinese martial underground known as Wulin. As a result, puppets, secret sects, powerful god-like creatures, monstrous beasts, and much more prowl Wulin’s various biomes. I haven’t kept count, but there are a massive number of enemies to take down, both standard mob variants and bosses, and the game stays fresh throughout. It's even fresher when you consider how many weapons you can acquire on Soul’s journey.

Every weapon is wholly unique, like picking up a new character in a fighting game, each with its own moveset and abilities. Upgrading these weapons through various tiers unlocks additional abilities, and you can even Soul Temper weapons to add one final, game-changing ability or perk. A fully upgraded weapon can have a moveset that uses the majority of buttons on your controller. You can do the same with Phantom Edges, special tide-turning weapons with limited uses (before you build up additional charges). Combined with different accessories and medicine types, Phantom Blade Zero offers hundreds, perhaps thousands, of combat kit permutations. You can play as a drunken fighter who switches between sober, tipsy, and drunken states, with his range and damage output changing as a result; you can focus on a bleed build, ripping enemies to shreds with charged attacks that utilize Soul's own HP to deal extra damage (that can then be earned back with bleed); you can use lightning, wind, fire, and ice to create elemental storms against enemies, and you can use a sword that switches between different elemental states on command as well. You can also just pound enemies to pulp with Phantom Edge fists, too. I’ve struggled to stop using these fists since acquiring them because they’re so satisfying.

Forty-plus hours into Phantom Blade Zero, it feels like I’ve played as dozens of different Souls because I've discovered so many build types. S-Game smartly pushes you to try new builds and weapons as you get them, doling out generous upgrade materials and currency; it encourages you to try everything, and the next weapon might just become your new favorite.

Finding these materials (and additional fights) is great fun, too, because Phantom Blade Zero’s various open-area biomes are a genuine joy to explore. You are always rewarded for taking the optional path, and those rewards are always worthwhile. You might find a healthy pile of upgrade materials, or a boss with a weapon you’ll fall in love with. The way buildings, alleys, caves, cliffsides, and other environmental features weave in and out of each other evokes FromSoftware’s architectural design and the subsequent shortcut “aha!” moments.

That said, Phantom Blade Zero is definitively not a Soulslike, though you’d be forgiven for assuming as much given its challenging suite of bosses, interconnected world, and Phantom Bell checkpoints, which are this game’s equivalent of bonfires. However, its challenge is much more surmountable (with various difficulties and accessories to ease parry and dodge timing), and its world progression is materially different. Kill an enemy and it’s dead for good, which to my surprise, adds a sense of worldbuilding I didn’t know I wanted. Progression through this journey feels tangible because I’m actually removing traces of evil with my weapons, traces that don’t respawn when I interact with checkpoints. It’s a nice change of pace that narratively speaks to Soul’s efforts.

Along the way, countless reading materials shed light on Phantom Blade Zero’s intertwining stories, and tracking down the next memory, scroll, or book entry rewards you if you’re interested in the full picture of this Wuxia story. I’d argue the game’s story is its weakest element, but only when compared to the rest of the package. It doesn't break any new ground narratively, but it provides enough mystery and thrill to keep things moving. And while performances are great, talking to characters is still mostly just two people standing across from each other talking through a new quest. Fortunately, cutscenes pick up the slack with dramatic villains, heartfelt revelations, raw tension, and more.

Production value is high across the board, thanks to incredibly impressive animation and a beautiful rendering of this dark fantasy China. Faces are lifelike, nudging up just shy of the uncanny valley as close-ups reveal porous details, lip quivers, and more, bringing an excellent cast of Chinese performances to life. The English voice acting has its standouts, but Soul’s voice is boring, so I highly recommend the Chinese vocals.

Boss fights draw clear inspiration from Chinese cinema and boast a wondrous sense of awe and scale that only the best in the genre typically offer. There are a ton of bosses, too, with very few repeats (repeats do happen in segmented challenge trials), and it’s impressive to think back on just how many I defeated, and just how many of them delivered a unique fight. I appreciate the checkpoints between boss phases as well. There are so many bosses – nearing 100 or more if I had to guess – and having my progression saved through phases removes some of the repetition I often feel when, say, phase two of a boss continues to kill me and I have to blitz through phase one again and again before taking another stab at it.

That scale and on-screen excitement carry through almost every fight in the game, down to even the simplest mob fights, though these are starting to feel a touch repetitive as I’m barreling toward the game’s end. Soul moves like the world’s greatest martial artist, but your controller inputs make it happen. If you mash the attack button, it looks nice… but if you use each weapon’s prescribed inputs and abilities, Phantom Blade Zero delivers a level of detailed action I’ve seen in few other games. You direct the game’s action, and this lets you turn what might otherwise be just another group of fodder enemies into an electric bout of spectacle.

To say I greatly enjoy this game greatly undersells my feelings – writing this review-in-progress is frustrating because I want to get back to Phantom Blade Zero. I expect to reach credits in the coming days, so please be on the lookout for my final verdict this week.

Battlefield Studios is seemingly trying something different with Battlefield 6’s next patch, which everyone assumed would be a standard, mid-season update not intended to change the game significantly.

However, it appears that it may bring more to the game than we realised, enough that the developer sees it as an excuse to bring back the pre-launch Battlefield Labs testing initiative.

The December 9 patch kicks off the final phase of the game’s first season, which is set to take the game through the holidays and into the new year. We’ve known about its content for a while, and it’s definitely the lightest, compared to the two previous phases.

Battlefield Studios announced a host of new changes that will be included in the same patch, which are apparently significant enough to require player testing. The developer is reviving Battlefield Labs to help it do so, but only for three two-hour sessions, split across the game’s three main server regions (EU, NA, APAC).

All tests are scheduled for today, December 2, and they remain under NDA. Battlefield Labs is also sticking with PC as its chosen platform yet again, though you will be able to join through Steam this time, alongside the EA app.

The focus of the test will be on three key areas that the December 9 patch will be touching. First, there’s footstep audio, an issue that was really brought into focus with the launch of Redsec Battle Royale. You can expect to hear enemy footsteps from farther away, and intuitively know the type of surface they’re moving on.

The patch also brings another pass to hit registration and netcode, which BF Studios says should improve responsiveness in close-quarter situations. Finally, there are broader changes to other combat areas that the announcement didn’t elaborate on.

All testing will take place on Eastwood, and Operation Firestorm, rotating between Conquest, and Escalation.

Going forward, Battlefield Studios said to expect Labs to be open to more players, and for the process itself to be smoother. The developer wants to have faster turnaround times, after all, so that the initiative can test smaller changes and be more responsive to player feedback.

Some of the more involved, future sessions will include experiments with map layout changes and various other non-standard compositions of player and vehicle numbers. Of course, you can also expect new maps and modes to be tested in Labs, similar to how the CTE was used in Battlefield 4’s long life.

#4370. Killer Klowns From Outer Space Almost Collabed With Dead Rising And Twisted Metal

A reliable Killer Klowns from Outer Space dataminer and news source has revealed that the game planned to include crossovers with Dead Rising, Twisted Metal, and Spawn.

As great as Dead by Daylight is, it’s fair to say that it’s caused a pretty big problem in the world of horror games, as nearly every property wants a slice of its sweet asymmetrical multiplayer pie. Sadly, even if they’re as good as The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, they can never really keep up and always end in the same barely functional, online only state.

Killer Klowns from Outer Space might not be as recognisable as Texas, but it’s another great example of a really good online game that has sadly been on its deathbed for a while. It was already a shame since it’s a genuinely great multiplayer experience, but it’s even more depressing now that we know what developer IllFonic had planned.

Over on Twitter, reliable dataminer and Killer Klowns from Outer Space news source (yes, that’s a thing) KKFOGameLeaks shared what has to be the game’s biggest leak to date. According to the game files, IllFonic planned to crossover with three pretty notable and thematically fitting series - Dead Rising, Twisted Metal, and Spawn.

Dead Rising Deluxe Remaster is the best way to play Frank West’s adventure, but I’ll never forget my first time.

Let’s give into my lifelong bias and start off with Dead Rising first, which would have added Adam from the first game and his brother Evan from Off the Record. That’s particularly interesting since the pair were never shown together in Dead Rising itself, and their moveset, consisting of hat lifts, chainsaw clashes, ice cream, and stilts, sounds perfect.

Then there’s who I would argue most people are interested in - Sweet Tooth from Twisted Metal. The game files suggest he would have had moves to do with his car, fire breath, an ice cream cone, and his iconic machete. The account even shared some concept art for Sweet Tooth in Killer Klowns, which is surprisingly dated back to 2021, a year before the game was revealed.

Twisted Metal fans really can’t have anything but the surprisingly good show, huh?

Rounding out the crossover clown car is Violator from Spawn, who seems to have been mostly inspired by the animated series thanks to the maggot ice cream mentioned in his files. I don’t know Spawn nearly as well as the other two collabs planned, but it seems like fans are really gutted it didn’t end up happening.

While crossovers are all the rage and not at all surprising for a big online game, it is interesting to see how dedicated IllFonic was to the bit by only having clown-themed characters. While Killer Klowns from Outer Space hasn’t been taken offline just yet, it’s incredibly low player count (eight concurrent on Steam as of the time of writing) means we’ll likely never see any of it come to light.

We finally got a chance to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and it's still one of the best games ever made.

#4369. Grammy Award-Winning Composer Austin Wintory Shares His Early Musical Drafts Intended For Mass Effect 5

Last week, EA shut down Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer BioWare, which resulted in the cancellation of the fifth Mass Effect game that was announced in 2020. As the fallout from this closure settles, famed video game composer Austin Wintory has shared that he'd been working on a potential soundtrack for the now-canceled game and has publicly released early versions of this score.

In a Bluesky thread, Wintory, who has composed soundtracks for games such as Journey, Sword of the Sea (for which he won a Grammy), Assassin’s Creed: Syndicate, and The Banner Saga trilogy, writes, “Mass Effect was my ultimate white whale, my all-time dream project. For the last couple years I'd been in discussion w/ BioWare & EA to take on the project & as part of that I wrote close to 20 minutes of music to explore where the franchise can go next, may as well share it!"

Wintory uploaded a 20-minute video consisting of eight tracks to his YouTube channel. The video begins with a message further elaborating on the partnership between BioWare, EA, and him. “For the past several years, I’d been in dialogue with people both at BioWare and EA to potentially jump into Mass Effect 5. As part of these conversations, I decided to surprise the team by writing/recording a gigantic love letter to the franchise, with my idea of where it can go next.”

Wintory adds that he composed the music in 2025 and that he “knew nothing” about what Mass Effect 5's story entailed when he did. As such, he describes the music as “narratively speculative.” He adds that this conceptual soundtrack was a direct homage to Jack Wall and Sam Hulick’s soundtrack on the first Mass Effect “while leaning even harder on true analog synths, and a more complex integration of the orchestra (almost akin to the hybrid nature of The Matrix),” he writes. Each music track features a message by Wintory explaining his inspiration for its production.

“Receiving the news alongside everyone else that EA had decided to not only cancel the project but shutdown BioWare entirely was a deeply felt loss," Wintory writes in the video's description. "It's been hard to see dear friends lose their jobs, and this beloved franchise seemingly vanish forever. Thank you nonetheless to everyone at BioWare and EA's music department for gifting me the chance to dream in your sandbox. It was a privilege to do even that much.”

Wintory's music is the latest piece of potential Mass Effect 5 content to emerge since BioWare’s closure. A day after the shutdown announcement, an unreleased but reportedly legitimate cinematic trailer for the canceled Mass Effect leaked online.

#4367. 7 Underrated JRPGs Released Against Huge AAA Launches

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

When Grand Theft Auto VI finally announced its release date, it was quite amusing to watch a flurry of other games sprint away from the November window, pushing their launches to either September or October. It packed those two months to the brim, but the move was completely understandable. Unless you are a colossal, iconic title like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, steering clear of a GTA release is simply logical.

With that in mind, I looked into a few games that lacked the marketing foresight to avoid massive AAA releases and ended up buried beneath mainstream hype. To keep things focused, I zeroed in on JRPGs. Today, I am highlighting several underrated JRPGs that never achieved the success they deserved, largely because all eyes were on massive blockbusters landing right alongside them.

Nothing beats casually picking up a title with no expectations, only to be completely blown away by the end.

While this list doesn't claim deep theoretical research connecting the sales data of every paired release, the comparison makes for a fascinating exercise.

The World Ends with You feels like one of those experimental projects from an era when Square Enix loved to innovate for its own sake. It was stylish, set in Shibuya, and had every ingredient to become a Nintendo DS hallmark, complete with character designs from peak-era Tetsuya Nomura. The game launched in Japan in 2007, but it only reached Western shores in April 2008, specifically on April 22.

Do you know what launched on April 29, just one week later? Grand Theft Auto IV, which was already one of the most anticipated games in industry history. Rockstar's powerhouse moved 3.6 million units on day one and 6 million in its first week, staggering figures for that generation. Naturally, the core audience buying GTA IV doesn't always overlap with players hunting down obscure JRPGs like The World Ends with You. Still, the real issue was media attention and marketing bandwidth. With the entire world talking about Liberty City, poor Neku barely stood a chance at making headlines.

This entry cuts a little too close to home. When I bought my PS3, I could only afford two games, and my final choice came down to Valkyria Chronicles versus Grand Theft Auto IV. Since I knew very little about Valkyria Chronicles and PS3 games were expensive, I took the safer bet, a decision I regret to this day. GTA IV was fantastic, but my JRPG-loving heart should have given Valkyria Chronicles the home it deserved.

The game did spawn several sequels over time, yet it remained criminally underrated and underappreciated in general gaming discourse. It performed well in Japan and exceeded SEGA's internal expectations, but Western sales were a different story. Valkyria Chronicles launched on November 4 in North America, right alongside Fallout 3 and LittleBigPlanet. While LittleBigPlanet might not sound like direct competition on paper, when forced to choose between an unproven new IP and safer mainstream hits, most players made the exact choice I did.

I know The Last Remnant doesn't boast a massive fanbase, but I consider it deeply underrated, especially for SaGa fans. It is atypical, a bit weird, and carries its fair share of flaws, but it remains a fascinating JRPG. Even its remaster failed to garner the accolades it deserved. I understand the game was part of Microsoft's broader effort to make the Xbox 360 a viable console in Japan, but the Western release strategy could have used serious fine-tuning.

The Last Remnant arrived on November 20, 2008. Just one week earlier, the gaming world received Call of Duty: World at War, and on Xbox, Call of Duty was king. Players were so deeply hooked on multiplayer matchmaking that everything else disappeared from their radar for a month. To make matters worse, Left 4 Dead landed right around the same time. Even as a new IP, it carried Valve's pedigree and Xbox 360 console exclusivity. The poor team behind The Last Remnant should have delayed the game just to give it a fighting chance.

Eternal Sonata was another JRPG born on the Xbox 360 to captivate the Japanese audience, launching there on June 14, 2007. In North America, the title landed on September 17, 2007, roughly a week before Halo 3. If Microsoft genuinely wanted to draw attention to Eternal Sonata, launching it right next to their biggest flagship IP was far from ideal.

These forgotten Xbox 360 RPGs came from some of gaming's big developers, including a Monster Hunter game no one remembers!

In my eyes, Eternal Sonata remains one of the most underrated JRPGs of all time. It is magnificent, deeply musical, features an impressive combat system, and looks gorgeous. Unfortunately, even when it was eventually ported to the PS3, it never achieved widespread commercial success. As a side note, Eternal Sonata sits on the GOG Dreamlist, so if you want a chance to play it on modern platforms, I highly recommend voting for it.

Claiming a Wii U game failed to reach its full potential because of competing software can feel a bit far-fetched, given that the console itself struggled globally. Still, examining who ate up the market share around Xenoblade Chronicles X remains a worthy exercise. As someone who has played JRPGs for three decades, I didn't even realize Chronicles X existed when it launched.

Xenoblade Chronicles X released in Japan on April 29, enjoying a modest run of around 100,000 copies sold that year. In North America, it launched on December 4. While Nintendo avoided direct clashes with a few mega-releases, the game still landed in the middle of the crowded holiday shopping season. November 2015 saw heavy hitters like Fallout 4, Call of Duty: Black Ops III, and Star Wars Battlefront. Surprisingly, the title actually performed better in North America than in Japan, which was a welcome silver lining.

This comparison might seem a little skewed on the surface, since owning a Switch in 2022 meant you weren't playing Elden Ring or Gran Turismo 7 on that specific hardware anyway. But the core question remains: would a player invest in a Switch title, or put their money toward the major releases on other platforms? As someone who doesn't care for racing games or FromSoftware's punishing difficulty, I personally favored Triangle Strategy, though I recognize that put me in the minority.

Triangle Strategy launched on March 4, 2022, just a week after Elden Ring, and we all know how that went. The entire internet entered full Elden Ring mode, dissecting its secrets and marveling at Hidetaka Miyazaki's world design. To top it off, Gran Turismo 7 released on the exact same day as Triangle Strategy. Even if you are not a racing fan, never underestimate GT's commercial power, as the seventh entry is rapidly approaching 13 million copies sold.

I vividly remember when Square Enix announced Star Ocean: The Divine Force, because a friend and I debated whether to buy it or Valkyrie Elysium, which Square Enix had launched just a month earlier. Buying games here in Brazil is practically a second job because of the high prices, so we have to study our options carefully before picking our poison. Luckily, I opted for The Divine Force upon its October 27, 2022 release, and it proved to be a great JRPG, especially compared to Valkyrie Elysium.

If I were torn between two niche JRPGs, imagine the broader audience looking at Call of Duty: Modern Warfare II, which launched the very next day, or God of War Ragnarök, which dropped two weeks later. Faced with a choice between Star Ocean and two of the industry's biggest franchises, it is easy to see which path the casual gamer took. You can hardly blame them either: time and money are limited resources.

While some JRPGs disappear, others return from oblivion after years without new releases.

#4366. Honkai: Star Rail 3.8 will run for an extra two weeks while Version 4.0 is in the oven

The next Honkai: Star Rail update is upon us, and there's a mix of good - and unusual news.

HoYoverse just hosted a sizeable Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, revealing more than just the game’s next major update. Version 3.8 was the big highlight, of course, with the new release arriving soon, on December 16-17 depending on your server region.

Alongside showing everything coming with this next update, the developer also announced that 3.8 will go on for eight weeks, rather than the usual six. V3.8 is dubbed "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams", and it brings an end to the Amphoreus journey.

The story in "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams" takes place after the final battle of Amphoreus, where Constance "The Dahlia" appears to deliver a twist: the Trailblazer's memories are scattered, with many parts missing.

This final quest revolves around finding them in order to piece together the mystery, and involves a return to Penacony. This memory-hunting adventure is told from the perspective of Firefly, which will also explain how she entered the dreamscape initially and met the squad.

The new playable character is The Dahlia, whose power is linked to the the Remembrance path, which allows her to fabricate memories. Despite taking her powers from the Remembrance, The Dhalia actually follows the Path of Nihility in-game: she’s a 5-Star character who shines in teams dealing Break DMG.

The Dhalia can unleash a Gloomy Zone that causes Toughness Reduction inflicted by allies to trigger Super Break DMG, even before you break your enemies’ Weaknesses. The Dahlia can also invite one teammate to become her Dance Partner, which allows them (and her) to deal additional Super Break DMG each time they attack an enemy. If you trigger her Ultimate after picking a Dance Partner, she applies Type Weaknesses of both partners to enemies.

While The Dahlia is the only new character appearing in this final Amphoreus update, there'll be reruns aplenty, with an unusual third banner phase to make up for the extra long wait for 4.0. Appropriately for her role in the story, Firefly will make her return alongside The Dahlia in Phase 1, while Fugue and Lingsha will both have banner reruns in Phase 2, which is expected on January 7th. A bonus two-week-long Phase 3 will then begin on January 28th, seeing brief reappearances for popular returning characters Aglaea and Sunday, before things (presumably) go back to normal with the new annual update.

Something else to look forward to in 3.8 is The Chrysos Awoo Championship, which invites players to become chimera trainers and compete in team-based battles. The Remnants of Twilight event kicks off with the new patch, too, featuring its own set of challenges. However, HoYoverse have confirmed that there won't be an extra event during Phase 3 — but hopefully that'll give you some time to wrap up the last of the Amphoreus story content, which is longer than the previous four chapters put together.

#4364. Free-To-Play MOBA Pokémon Unite Is Shutting Down In March

The free-to-play MOBA Pokémon Unite will shut down in March, over five years after its 2021 launch. Although a gradual suspension of services begins today, fans will enjoy one last hurrah thanks to a big in-game event running for the remainder of the game’s lifecycle.

Launched in July 2021 for Switch before migrating to iOS and Android later that year, Pokémon Unite was billed as a friendlier take on the MOBA genre popularized by Dota 2 and League of Legends, thanks to its short matches (10 minutes) and simplified mechanics. Despite its initial popularity, the game is winding down and will go offline for good on March 23, 2027.

An End of Service notice on the game’s website reads,

“We offer our sincerest gratitude to the many Trainers who have played since service started for the Nintendo Switch version on July 21, 2021. We would like to express our thanks to everyone by holding a special event until service ends. The Pokémon Unite Aeos Crown 2027 Tokyo competitive tournament (an event for Pokémon Unite only) will also be held as previously announced. We hope you continue to enjoy Pokémon Unite until the final day of service. After service ends, the 'Pokémon Unite Game Content Guidelines for Online Platforms' will no longer be published or maintained, and we will no longer provide support regarding use of Pokémon Unite videos and images.”

As of today, in-game sales of Aeos gems and Unite Club memberships/renewals have been suspended. Existing Unite Club members will continue to use their benefits until the end of the membership period.

On November 12, an update will kick off the aforementioned final special event, where players can obtain items such as all Unite licenses and Holoware that have appeared in the game up to that point. A library feature will also be added, letting players view certain records and in-game content even after the game shuts down on March 23. Those who don’t download the library feature before the shutdown date will not be able to get it afterward.

Qualifiers for the Aeos Crown 2027 Tokyo Competitive tournament will take place as planned on December 5. After the game shuts down on March 23, players won't be able to log in to Pokémon Unite or play any battles. Only the library feature will remain accessible.

We enjoyed Pokémon Unite when it launched, with executive video editor Alex Van Aken scoring it an 8 out of 10 in his review, writing, “The game eats away the hours of my day as I reassuringly say to myself, 'Just one more match.' Battles play out with the spectacle that the Pokémon series is known for, and with so many abilities to choose from, no match feels the same as the last. The game’s simple mechanics and recognizable characters make for an approachable MOBA experience, and with a potential catalog of nearly 900 Pokémon to pick from, my hopes are high for the future of Pokémon Unite.”

#4363. Tomorrow’s Battlefield 6 patch is the first step towards improving footstep audio, and it might actually fix the settings reset bug

The next major Battlefield 6 patch is nearly upon us, and Battlefield Studios is promising a bounty of changes - including a couple of fixes to some big bugs.

Battlefield 6 is about to receive a new update. Version 1.1.3.0 is set to arrive tomorrow, December 9 to kick off the third and final phase of the game’s first season. Winter Offensive brings some holiday-themed new content to the game, but it’s not the most interesting part of the patch.

That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the new patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.

Thew new content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly. To go along with that there are new limited-time modes for both multiplayer and Redsec’s Gauntlet. The event mode will be available in Conquest, and Domination.

The Ice Climbing Axe is the only new weapon in this drop. The battle pass gets a new Winter Offensive bonus path, just like we’ve seen with previous seasonal stages. This is how you unlock the axe, too.

Easily the most interesting change in this update is the range of improvements to audio across the board. First, footstep audio received a big pass that should make it easier to hear enemy footsteps, easier to locate them, and across different surfaces.

Some of the bugs that caused certain sounds to simply vanish have been fixed. This was especially prevalent in battle royale matches. BF Studios explained in the patch notes that it has adjusted memory priorities for in-game sounds in order to prioritise the most crucial ones. This is not the end of the road on audio, however, as the developer continues to work on making the soundscape more stable and reliable.

Some of those audio changes are the result of recent testing done in Battlefield Labs, which is also responsible for another exciting addition in this latest patch: improvements to hit registration.

While BF6 has had solid and stable netcode, certain situations would sometimes create uncertainty about how you died, and why certain actions seemingly failed to perform at that particular moment.

The focus in this update is to improve the reliability of how actions in close-quarter combat are translated, which includes firing before fully going into ADS, quick aim changes and more.

Speaking of close-range, the patch also brings another pass to soldier visibility to make it easier for enemies to stand out from the background. This is particularly relevant in areas with low contrast, or busy environments with lots of particle and visual effects.

1.1.3.0 also brings yet another set of weapon handling and gunplay tweaks, this time focusing on accuracy issues with first shots. You can also expect more tweaks to attachment behaviour with regards to recoil.

Something else worth highlighting is that vehicle gameplay is getting several smaller tweaks that have to do with how they interact with the world, how their HUDs behave and more. Finally, your settings should no longer be reset after applying an update. BF Studios says there are still some instances where that might happen, but the issue should be fixed for the majority of players.

You can read the full change log on the Battlefield blog.

#4360. Phantom Blade Zero Review – Wuxia Wonder Abounds

Rooted in Wuxian storytelling and scale, built on an impressively detailed combat system, and wrapped in a bloody Chinese martial underground that’s a genuine joy to play in, Phantom Blade Zero is a feat. It joins an echelon of action pedigree that includes Sekiro, Devil May Cry, Bayonetta, and just about any other action game you hold in high regard. It hails from developer S-Game, which has dabbled in mobile and smaller-scale games, and I’m shocked by what it’s pulled off with its triple-A action inauguration. But make no mistake: though Phantom Blade Zero is this team’s first crack at a game like this, it is an incredibly confident, strong debut.

Protagonist Soul is a stoic martial arts master betrayed by the Order he’s sworn his life to; he dies and returns to life with only 66 days to live. That’s enough time to settle his debts, repay his betrayers, and end a villainous conspiracy to seize full power of the Wulin realm. This narrative is Phantom Blade Zero's weakest link, but its premise adds enough mystery and tension to keep this Wuxian journey exciting through to its final, realm-shattering moments. Narrative bombshells drop not just through the game’s general fantasy-realism art direction, but also through anime scenes, opera puppet shows, animated brushstroke sequences, and more, highlighting Chinese culture and its integral place in Phantom Blade Zero.

The game features a staggering number of unique enemy types, and though the final hours get a bit repetitive, it’s admirable how long S-Game maintains such a high level of combat-oriented ecstasy. Soul’s access to weapons drives that exhilaration. Every weapon is wholly unique. Because the combat is combo-based, picking up a new weapon feels like unlocking a new character in a fighting game. Each has its own moveset and abilities, with later-game weapons featuring combo lists that look more at home in a Street Fighter menu. Add in the special, tide-turning weapons known as Phantom Edges, with limited charge-based uses, and there’s no shortage of permutations to delightfully experiment with.

Drawing on Chinese cinema, Phantom Blade Zero's setpiece bosses boast a sense of awe and scale only the genre's best typically offer. With virtually no repeat bosses, save for a few in separate trials, it’s impressive how many powerful figures I flayed, and how many delivered a unique fight. I also appreciate the checkpoints between boss phases, as they remove the frustrating repetition of replaying phase one again and again just to take another stab at the second phase I’m struggling with.

You’d be forgiven for assuming Phantom Blade Zero is a Soulslike, given its challenging bosses, interconnected world, and Phantom Bell checkpoints, this game’s equivalent of bonfires. It definitively isn’t, though. The challenge is much more surmountable; the game isn’t interested in making you die over and over, there are difficulty options, and you can equip accessories to make parries and dodges easier. World progression is materially different, too, as enemies don’t respawn after you kill them. It’s an interesting, perhaps blasphemous, choice for the genre, but it's surprisingly effective, adding a sense of worldbuilding and tangible progression I didn’t know I wanted from my action games. Soul is on a mission to remove evil, and mechanically, I’m doing just that. Enemies don’t respawn incoherently just because I heal and save.

Environmental features weave in and out of each other, and the architectural design and layout of these regions lead to many subsequent “aha” moments. S-Game infuses search-action elements into this exploration through the aforementioned Phantom Edges, some of which double as tools to unlock surprising new areas in both new and previously visited biomes. As a result, backtracking and exploration remain fresh. A lot of it is optional, as are some of Phantom Blade Zero's most rewarding elements, including its demanding “perfect” ending. Sadly, this renders other endings unsatisfying, with clear chunks intentionally missing.

Despite forays into the Uncanny Valley, Phantom Blade Zero is visually striking, and the action is brilliantly animated. It’s all set to genre-breaking music, too, with original metalcore songs, operatic choirs, 808s, and traditional Chinese instrumentation, creating a score as illustrious as the action it enhances.

Phantom Blade Zero is an astounding action achievement, almost unbelievably so for a game that is essentially a studio’s genre debut. It is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, one that recognizes the genre’s strengths and weaknesses and addresses both with fantastical Wuxian style. Though the action genre is always jam-packed with new releases, few are as special as Phantom Blade Zero.
